title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians
description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority,  and is published that it may go down to posterity.”  

The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.

But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting. No extant copies could be found.

The debate over the authenticity of the Mecklenburg Declaration began. And, when a copy of a document called the Mecklenburg Resolves written on May 30, 1775, was discovered in a 1775 newspaper, the debate intensified. The Resolves were revolutionary, but stopped short of declaring independence. Did both documents exist? Or was the Declaration being conflated with the Resolves?

Examine the evidence and decide for yourself by visiting the new exhibit, “Mecklenburg Declaration?” at the Presbyterian Heritage Center.

The PHC is open Tuesday-Friday (10-4) and Saturday (12-4).

title: John and June Allcott Gallery: taylor barnes, Weight of Light
location: Hanes Art Center, John and June Allcott Gallery
description:
Reception and artist conversation: October 29, 2026, 5:00 pm

 

Weight of Light is an exhibition of seven works by multidisciplinary artist taylor barnes, created during her year-long residency at West Orchid in Pine Lake, Georgia. Weight of Light considers the relationship between material, perception, and the ongoing process of becoming. Emerging from a period of experimentation and personal reflection, the works occupy an ambiguous space between painting and object. Neither fixed representations nor resolved compositions, the works function as thresholds—sites of transition where questions of origin, transformation, and self-possession remain open.

 

barnes approaches the canvas as a material structure rather than a passive surface. Through staining, layering, saturation, and the transformation of matter between solid and liquid states, she explores the physical and conceptual possibilities of charcoal. Materials shift, settle, resist, and respond, creating conditions in which chance, absence, and emergence become integral to the work. The works do not seek resolution through conventional notions of completion. Instead, they retain evidence of their making—gestures, interruptions, accumulations, and erasures that reveal the instability and possibility inherent in transformation. What remains visible is a record of decisions, encounters, and material negotiations. The works resist linear narratives of progress, suggesting instead a cyclical understanding of origin, movement, and revelation. Abstract maps, they trace an unfolding relationship between the known and obscured. Darkness and light emerge not as opposing forces, but as interdependent conditions which continually refigure perception and understanding. Black, the central color and philosophical foundation of barnes' practice, becomes a space of depth, presence, and possibility—a means of considering how material holds identity, memory, and lived experience. Informed by bell hooks' writings on objectification and subjectivity, barnes' work engages questions of agency, visibility, and the reclamation of self. Ultimately, Weight of Light proposes ascension not as transcendence or arrival, but as an ongoing practice of self-possession. Through material experimentation and an embrace of uncertainty, barnes creates space for the possibility that becoming is neither linear nor complete, but continually negotiated through acts of making, unmaking, and reclamation.

 

taylor barnes is a multidisciplinary artist working across ceramics, fibers, and drawing. Her practice investigates spirituality, oral history, and structures of power through material and form. Working primarily with clay, fabric, string, and charcoal, she translates emotion and lived experience into material forms that hold traces of labor, memory, and ritual. barnes received her MFA in Fibers from the University of North Texas. She lives and works between Georgia and Austin, Texas.

 

Admission: Free

Gallery Hours: Monday-Friday, 8 am-5 pm

 

A weeknight or daytime permit is now required after 5:00 pm on weekdays. No permit is required from 5:00 pm Friday through 7:30 am Monday. A $1.00 one-night pass is available in selected lots. More information can be found HERE.

 

Artist website: https://www.barnesartistry.com/ 

 

For more information, please contact: Annette Lawrence, annettel@unc.edu

An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.

But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting. No extant copies could be found.

The debate over the authenticity of the Mecklenburg Declaration began. And, when a copy of a document called the Mecklenburg Resolves written on May 30, 1775, was discovered in a 1775 newspaper, the debate intensified. The Resolves were revolutionary, but stopped short of declaring independence. Did both documents exist? Or was the Declaration being conflated with the Resolves?

Examine the evidence and decide for yourself by visiting the new exhibit, “Mecklenburg Declaration?” at the Presbyterian Heritage Center.

The PHC is open Tuesday-Friday (10-4) and Saturday (12-4).

title: Project RESTORE Educator Trek: Waterdog Warriors
location: Nature Exploration Center, 11 West Jones Street, Raleigh, NC, 27601, United States
description:
Date: Saturday, December 5, 2026. Please also mark your calendar for a rain date on Sunday, December 6!
Times: 9am to 5pm 
Join us in the search for one of North Carolina’s rarest salamanders, the federally threatened Neuse River waterdog, found only in the Neuse and Tar-Pamlico River Basins in North Carolina. Learn from expert biologists, explore the natural history of the waterdog, observe historically collected specimens and participate in field monitoring of the species. Discover how you can bring the excitement of field research of this rare species into your classroom. 
With support from the US Fish and Wildlife Service, Project RESTORE (Rescuing Endangered Species Through Outreach, Restoration, and Education) will feature a suite of educational opportunities for teachers and students to participate in restoration and monitoring of imperiled and endangered species in eastern North Carolina.

title: Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage
description: Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage at the Gregg Museum of Art & Design presents a series of vignettes exploring spaces of dignity, belonging, safety, and imagination within Black communities across North Carolina. Featuring historical photographs, contemporary images, artworks from the Gregg Museum collection including a handmade guitar by Freeman Vines, and ephemera from community partners, the exhibition reflects on place, memory, creativity, and spiritual resilience across generations. Through stories of triumph and adversity, Community Stories honors the ways Black Americans have sustained and uplifted their communities through family, entrepreneurship, cultural expression, and soulful imagination, while inspiring future generations.

title: NC State LIVE Well-Being Concerts With Nnenna and Pierce Freelon
location: Gregg Museum of Art & Design, Galleries and Main Lobby
description:
NC State LIVE and the Gregg Museum of Art & Design have partnered to present Well-Being Concerts, featuring a family with rich connections to the university and the museum. The late architect Phil Freelon, an NC State College of Design alumnus, led the team that designed the Gregg’s new home, which opened in 2017. Phil Freelon's widow and son, Nnenna and Pierce Freelon, are a Grammy-nominated mother-son musical duo known for their collaborative children’s album, AnceStars. Nnenna Freelon is an acclaimed composer, podcaster, author and advocate for arts education. In addition to his music career, Pierce Freelon is a picture book author, podcaster and ice cream maker. The duo will perform at the Gregg inside the gallery featuring the exhibition Grounded by artist-in-residence Maya Freelon, Phil and Nnenna Freelon’s daughter. Shaped by Maya Freelon’s personal and collective memory, ancestry and humanity, Grounded transforms the Gregg into a retrospective on well-being, connection and discovery. 

This concert was created in partnership with Carnegie Hall’s Weill Music Institute. Carnegie Hall’s Well-Being Concerts combine world-class musical performances with elements of self-care and mindfulness, animated by evidence that music helps people heal and thrive.
source: NC State Gregg Museum of Art & Design

title: Dorrance Dance The Nutcracker Suite
description:
Holiday traditions have a way of bringing people together. The best ones feel familiar and fresh at the same time.

 

Dorrance Dance‘s The Nutcracker Suite is set to Duke Ellington and Billy Strayhorn’s extraordinary 1960 reinterpretation of the Tchaikovsky score. Part seasonal concert, part tap ballet, the production transforms the Sugar Plum Fairy into a slinky Sugar Rum Cherry, turns the “March of the Toy Soldiers” into a swinging brass “Peanut Brittle Brigade,” and gives the original ballet’s pageant of national dances a fresh 21st-century twist. 

 

Drawing on the rich traditions of tap dance to tell the story of one of the most beloved works in the holiday canon, The Nutcracker Suite is filled with rhythm, virtuosity, humor, and heart. The result is a performance that celebrates the joy of tradition while reminding us that the stories we return to year after year still evolve.

 

Student tickets always $11. Eligible for CLE. Find out more and buy tickets at: https://carolinaperformingarts.org/events/thenutcrackersuite/

title: Gathering: A Collaborative Nature Art Experience for the Cancer Community
location: Duke Gardens–Barnes Welcome Center, 420 Anderson Street, Durham, NC, 27705, United States
description:
Offered in collaboration with Dr. Kristin Huang, a clinical psychologist and cancer survivor whose work explores the intersections of psychology, creativity, nature and human development. 
Join us at Duke Gardens for an afternoon of creativity and connection for people whose lives have been touched by cancer. Using flowers, leaves, branches and other natural materials, participants will create temporary designs on individual panels. There is no right way to make them, and no art experience is needed. The invitation is simply to slow down, work with the natural materials and create something that feels meaningful to you. Individual panels will be brought together in a large, quilt-like installation, transforming many distinct creations into a shared work of art. Weather permitting, the completed installation will be assembled outdoors on the Gateway Gardens Event Lawn, offering a chance to step back and experience what we have created together. Gathering is less about making something permanent than about the experience of making: noticing beauty, experimenting, reflecting and allowing space to discover what emerges. Each piece stands on its own while also becoming part of something larger—a fitting expression of the individuality and shared connection within the cancer community. All materials will be provided. No art experience is necessary. 
Fee: Free; registration recommended. 
Parking: Parking fees apply. 
Location: Meet at the Barnes Welcome Center 
Accessibility: This program takes place indoors and outdoors, in areas accessible via paved paths, with accessible restrooms available nearby. Please note that program supplies include natural plant materials.

title: Service of Remembrance for James Seay
description:
A service of remembrance for the late poet and longtime UNC-Chapel Hill writing professor James (Jim) Seay will be held on Sunday, December 6th, 2026, at 2 p.m. at the Horace Williams House in Chapel Hill.  Professor Seay, who taught at Carolina from 1974 till 2014, died in Chapel Hill in July at the age of 87.

 

 

A native Mississippian, Seay was a vigorous outdoorsman, fisherman and hunter, and wrote of his ventures afield in his last book of essays, Come! Come! Where? Where? (UNC Press). He was well and widely known for his celebrated volumes of poetry, including:  Let Not Your Heart (1970), Water Tables (1974), The Light as They Found It (1990), and Open Field, Understory (1997). In 1988 he received the Award in Literature from the American Academy of Arts and Letters.

 

The December 6th service will be conducted by UNC’s Creative Writing Program (which Professor Seay directed 1987-1997) and the Department of English and Comparative Literature.

title: John and June Allcott Gallery: taylor barnes, Weight of Light
location: Hanes Art Center, John and June Allcott Gallery
description:
Reception and artist conversation: October 29, 2026, 5:00 pm

 

Weight of Light is an exhibition of seven works by multidisciplinary artist taylor barnes, created during her year-long residency at West Orchid in Pine Lake, Georgia. Weight of Light considers the relationship between material, perception, and the ongoing process of becoming. Emerging from a period of experimentation and personal reflection, the works occupy an ambiguous space between painting and object. Neither fixed representations nor resolved compositions, the works function as thresholds—sites of transition where questions of origin, transformation, and self-possession remain open.

 

barnes approaches the canvas as a material structure rather than a passive surface. Through staining, layering, saturation, and the transformation of matter between solid and liquid states, she explores the physical and conceptual possibilities of charcoal. Materials shift, settle, resist, and respond, creating conditions in which chance, absence, and emergence become integral to the work. The works do not seek resolution through conventional notions of completion. Instead, they retain evidence of their making—gestures, interruptions, accumulations, and erasures that reveal the instability and possibility inherent in transformation. What remains visible is a record of decisions, encounters, and material negotiations. The works resist linear narratives of progress, suggesting instead a cyclical understanding of origin, movement, and revelation. Abstract maps, they trace an unfolding relationship between the known and obscured. Darkness and light emerge not as opposing forces, but as interdependent conditions which continually refigure perception and understanding. Black, the central color and philosophical foundation of barnes' practice, becomes a space of depth, presence, and possibility—a means of considering how material holds identity, memory, and lived experience. Informed by bell hooks' writings on objectification and subjectivity, barnes' work engages questions of agency, visibility, and the reclamation of self. Ultimately, Weight of Light proposes ascension not as transcendence or arrival, but as an ongoing practice of self-possession. Through material experimentation and an embrace of uncertainty, barnes creates space for the possibility that becoming is neither linear nor complete, but continually negotiated through acts of making, unmaking, and reclamation.

 

taylor barnes is a multidisciplinary artist working across ceramics, fibers, and drawing. Her practice investigates spirituality, oral history, and structures of power through material and form. Working primarily with clay, fabric, string, and charcoal, she translates emotion and lived experience into material forms that hold traces of labor, memory, and ritual. barnes received her MFA in Fibers from the University of North Texas. She lives and works between Georgia and Austin, Texas.

 

Admission: Free

Gallery Hours: Monday-Friday, 8 am-5 pm

 

A weeknight or daytime permit is now required after 5:00 pm on weekdays. No permit is required from 5:00 pm Friday through 7:30 am Monday. A $1.00 one-night pass is available in selected lots. More information can be found HERE.

 

Artist website: https://www.barnesartistry.com/ 

 

For more information, please contact: Annette Lawrence, annettel@unc.edu

title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians
description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority,  and is published that it may go down to posterity.”  

The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.

But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting. No extant copies could be found.

The debate over the authenticity of the Mecklenburg Declaration began. And, when a copy of a document called the Mecklenburg Resolves written on May 30, 1775, was discovered in a 1775 newspaper, the debate intensified. The Resolves were revolutionary, but stopped short of declaring independence. Did both documents exist? Or was the Declaration being conflated with the Resolves?

Examine the evidence and decide for yourself by visiting the new exhibit, “Mecklenburg Declaration?” at the Presbyterian Heritage Center.

The PHC is open Tuesday-Friday (10-4) and Saturday (12-4).

title: John and June Allcott Gallery: taylor barnes, Weight of Light
location: Hanes Art Center, John and June Allcott Gallery
description:
Reception and artist conversation: October 29, 2026, 5:00 pm

 

Weight of Light is an exhibition of seven works by multidisciplinary artist taylor barnes, created during her year-long residency at West Orchid in Pine Lake, Georgia. Weight of Light considers the relationship between material, perception, and the ongoing process of becoming. Emerging from a period of experimentation and personal reflection, the works occupy an ambiguous space between painting and object. Neither fixed representations nor resolved compositions, the works function as thresholds—sites of transition where questions of origin, transformation, and self-possession remain open.

 

barnes approaches the canvas as a material structure rather than a passive surface. Through staining, layering, saturation, and the transformation of matter between solid and liquid states, she explores the physical and conceptual possibilities of charcoal. Materials shift, settle, resist, and respond, creating conditions in which chance, absence, and emergence become integral to the work. The works do not seek resolution through conventional notions of completion. Instead, they retain evidence of their making—gestures, interruptions, accumulations, and erasures that reveal the instability and possibility inherent in transformation. What remains visible is a record of decisions, encounters, and material negotiations. The works resist linear narratives of progress, suggesting instead a cyclical understanding of origin, movement, and revelation. Abstract maps, they trace an unfolding relationship between the known and obscured. Darkness and light emerge not as opposing forces, but as interdependent conditions which continually refigure perception and understanding. Black, the central color and philosophical foundation of barnes' practice, becomes a space of depth, presence, and possibility—a means of considering how material holds identity, memory, and lived experience. Informed by bell hooks' writings on objectification and subjectivity, barnes' work engages questions of agency, visibility, and the reclamation of self. Ultimately, Weight of Light proposes ascension not as transcendence or arrival, but as an ongoing practice of self-possession. Through material experimentation and an embrace of uncertainty, barnes creates space for the possibility that becoming is neither linear nor complete, but continually negotiated through acts of making, unmaking, and reclamation.

 

taylor barnes is a multidisciplinary artist working across ceramics, fibers, and drawing. Her practice investigates spirituality, oral history, and structures of power through material and form. Working primarily with clay, fabric, string, and charcoal, she translates emotion and lived experience into material forms that hold traces of labor, memory, and ritual. barnes received her MFA in Fibers from the University of North Texas. She lives and works between Georgia and Austin, Texas.

 

Admission: Free

Gallery Hours: Monday-Friday, 8 am-5 pm

 

A weeknight or daytime permit is now required after 5:00 pm on weekdays. No permit is required from 5:00 pm Friday through 7:30 am Monday. A $1.00 one-night pass is available in selected lots. More information can be found HERE.

title: Dec 8 - How to Let Long-tail Guide Your 3D Annotation Workshop
description:
Raleigh AI, Machine Learning and Computer Vision Meetup
Join us on Dec 8 for the “How to Let Long-tail Guide Your 3D Annotation” workshop with [Eric Hofesmann](https://www.linkedin.com/in/eric-hofesmann/).

**Date, Time and Location**

Dec 08, 2026
9:00 AM - 10:00 AM PST
Online. **[Register for the Zoom!](https://voxel51.com/events/how-to-let-long-tail-guide-your-3d-annotation-december-8-2026)**

Autonomous driving models rarely fail on the common case. They fail on the long-tail: the pedestrian stepping out from behind a parked truck or a construction zone that matches nothing in the training set. Each of those moments lives in synchronized multi-sensor data, made up of a LiDAR sweep, a ring of cameras, a timestamp, and a calibration. Fixing one means finding it, labeling it in 3D, and proving the next model handles it.

In this live session, we will take long-tail driving scenarios from discovery to 3D labels to evaluation, and make the case that 3D ground truth should be built where your data lives, not exported away from it.
source: Meetup: Raleigh AI, ML & Computer Vision

title: Durham Social Hack Night
description:
Triangle Developers
Hey tech folks, come out and hang at Hi-Wire starting at 6pm! Hack Night is meant to be a social evening for folks in tech. It's less about networking and more about community.

**Look for the Hack Night tabletop sign** and nerds wearing name tags to find us. If the weather is nice, we'll probably be outside.

Help folks feel welcome by using the **"Pac Man Rule"** \- when standing with a group of people \(usually in a circle\)\, leave some space open so that another person can easily join\.

See our [Code of Conduct](https://github.com/TriangleDevsSlack/policies/blob/master/code-of-conduct.md). To summarize: be nice or leave. No tolerance for harassment or oppression. In addition, since alcohol is present at these events, please be mindful of your consumption and respect other people's choices on whether or not to consume.

**FAQs**
*Do folks hack at Hack Night? Should I bring my computer?*
This is more of a night for hackers than an actual hack night. You're welcome to bring a laptop, but most people will only be socializing.

*What are the beverage options? Are there any non-alcoholic drinks?*
Hi-Wire Brewing offers many types of beers including a few non-alcoholic options plus wine and some liquor. They usually have a happy hour special on the first few beers on the menu. In the same complex are Cugino Forno which has additional drink options, and Two Roosters which has excellent ice cream.

*Are there any drink specials?*
If Hack Night is on a Tuesday, Hi-Wire usually has $5 pints for their flagship beers. Look for the list at the counter.

*Do people eat snacks/dinner during the meetup?*
Sometimes folks will order a pizza or salad from Cugino Forno. I sometimes grab an ice cream from Two Roosters across the way. Most people eat before or after but it's no big deal - whatever you prefer and are most comfortable with.

*How can I connect with the developer community?*
Go to [triangledevelopers.com](https://triangledevelopers.com/) to find the Discord and Slack info.

title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians
description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority,  and is published that it may go down to posterity.”  

The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.

But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting. No extant copies could be found.

The debate over the authenticity of the Mecklenburg Declaration began. And, when a copy of a document called the Mecklenburg Resolves written on May 30, 1775, was discovered in a 1775 newspaper, the debate intensified. The Resolves were revolutionary, but stopped short of declaring independence. Did both documents exist? Or was the Declaration being conflated with the Resolves?

Examine the evidence and decide for yourself by visiting the new exhibit, “Mecklenburg Declaration?” at the Presbyterian Heritage Center.

The PHC is open Tuesday-Friday (10-4) and Saturday (12-4).

title: John and June Allcott Gallery: taylor barnes, Weight of Light
location: Hanes Art Center, John and June Allcott Gallery
description:
Reception and artist conversation: October 29, 2026, 5:00 pm

 

Weight of Light is an exhibition of seven works by multidisciplinary artist taylor barnes, created during her year-long residency at West Orchid in Pine Lake, Georgia. Weight of Light considers the relationship between material, perception, and the ongoing process of becoming. Emerging from a period of experimentation and personal reflection, the works occupy an ambiguous space between painting and object. Neither fixed representations nor resolved compositions, the works function as thresholds—sites of transition where questions of origin, transformation, and self-possession remain open.

 

barnes approaches the canvas as a material structure rather than a passive surface. Through staining, layering, saturation, and the transformation of matter between solid and liquid states, she explores the physical and conceptual possibilities of charcoal. Materials shift, settle, resist, and respond, creating conditions in which chance, absence, and emergence become integral to the work. The works do not seek resolution through conventional notions of completion. Instead, they retain evidence of their making—gestures, interruptions, accumulations, and erasures that reveal the instability and possibility inherent in transformation. What remains visible is a record of decisions, encounters, and material negotiations. The works resist linear narratives of progress, suggesting instead a cyclical understanding of origin, movement, and revelation. Abstract maps, they trace an unfolding relationship between the known and obscured. Darkness and light emerge not as opposing forces, but as interdependent conditions which continually refigure perception and understanding. Black, the central color and philosophical foundation of barnes' practice, becomes a space of depth, presence, and possibility—a means of considering how material holds identity, memory, and lived experience. Informed by bell hooks' writings on objectification and subjectivity, barnes' work engages questions of agency, visibility, and the reclamation of self. Ultimately, Weight of Light proposes ascension not as transcendence or arrival, but as an ongoing practice of self-possession. Through material experimentation and an embrace of uncertainty, barnes creates space for the possibility that becoming is neither linear nor complete, but continually negotiated through acts of making, unmaking, and reclamation.

 

taylor barnes is a multidisciplinary artist working across ceramics, fibers, and drawing. Her practice investigates spirituality, oral history, and structures of power through material and form. Working primarily with clay, fabric, string, and charcoal, she translates emotion and lived experience into material forms that hold traces of labor, memory, and ritual. barnes received her MFA in Fibers from the University of North Texas. She lives and works between Georgia and Austin, Texas.

 

Admission: Free

Gallery Hours: Monday-Friday, 8 am-5 pm

 

A weeknight or daytime permit is now required after 5:00 pm on weekdays. No permit is required from 5:00 pm Friday through 7:30 am Monday. A $1.00 one-night pass is available in selected lots. More information can be found HERE.

Please join our virtual welcome session with this link

Are you a young person between 13 and 25 years old who is interested in taking action around preventing gun violence? Join us for our Team ENOUGH welcome session to learn more about the different ways you can engage. 

Team ENOUGH is a youth-led program whose mission is to educate young voices about gun violence and mobilize them to take meaningful action against it. Supported by Brady United, we harness the expertise and experience of today’s youth to advance our intersectional work across the country. 

Led by an Executive Council, comprised of students just like us, we believe that diversity is a strength, and that only when everyone has a seat at the table can we build an effective movement to prevent all gun violence in all communities.

For us, preventing gun violence not only requires regulating access to firearms but also addressing how systemic racism and environmental factors cause this form of bloodshed to run especially rampant in communities of color. You cannot talk about gun violence without talking about police brutality, white supremacy, the broken criminal justice system, poverty, homophobia, access to affordable housing, or the often barriers separating disadvantaged populations from physical and mental healthcare. 

So if you share this belief, join us for our Team ENOUGH welcome session and become part of the movement to end gun violence in our lifetime.

title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians
description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority,  and is published that it may go down to posterity.”  

The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.

But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting. No extant copies could be found.

The debate over the authenticity of the Mecklenburg Declaration began. And, when a copy of a document called the Mecklenburg Resolves written on May 30, 1775, was discovered in a 1775 newspaper, the debate intensified. The Resolves were revolutionary, but stopped short of declaring independence. Did both documents exist? Or was the Declaration being conflated with the Resolves?

Examine the evidence and decide for yourself by visiting the new exhibit, “Mecklenburg Declaration?” at the Presbyterian Heritage Center.

The PHC is open Tuesday-Friday (10-4) and Saturday (12-4).

description:
Raleigh AI, Machine Learning and Computer Vision Meetup
Join our virtual meetup to hear talks from experts on cutting-edge topics across AI, ML, and computer vision.

**Date, Time and Location**

Dec 10, 2026
9:00 AM - 11:00 AM PST
Online. **[Register for the Zoom!](https://voxel51.com/events/ai-ml-and-computer-vision-meetup-december-10-2026)**

**Your mAP is fine. Your slices are not. Finding the images that actually matter**

A single mAP can look acceptable while one slice is unusable, small objects, occlusion, or a confused class. I will run a pretrained detector on a few hundred public images (COCO-style, not a production crawl), report the headline metric, then break the same run by slice and walk through the worst samples.

The claim is modest: you do not need a million images or a trained-from-scratch model to see what the mean is hiding, and you cannot relabel everything, so the next labeling budget should follow those slices. No employer data and no confidential dashboards.

*About the Speaker*

[Amandeep Jiddewar](https://www.linkedin.com/in/amanfj/) is a Machine Learning Engineer at Pinterest, with prior work in U.S. manufacturing analytics (CertainTeed / Saint-Gobain) and marketplace allocation (QuinStreet). Emory Goizueta MSBA (2019), Kaggle Expert. This talk is in his personal capacity and does not represent his current or prior employers.

**Production AI Agents: Tool Use, Evaluation, Guardrails and Observability**

Building an AI agent is easy. Knowing whether it is behaving reliably in production is much harder. This session explores how to evaluate agents that use tools and external systems, including tool-call validation, tracing, observability, failure analysis, guardrails, permissions, and human review.

Attendees will learn practical patterns for understanding not just what an agent answered, but why it acted and whether the action was safe.

*About the Speaker*

[Akshay Talathi](https://www.linkedin.com/in/akshaytalathi/) is a Vice President at Goldman Sachs with over 10 years of experience building large-scale, cloud-native, and distributed systems across financial services and technology. His current focus is GenAI and agentic AI, including production AI agents, MCP, enterprise integrations, guardrails, observability, and reliable AI-driven workflows.

**From Virtual Worlds to Physical AI: Building Simulation Pipelines That Survive the Real World**

Robots are moving beyond perception systems that only detect and classify objects toward systems that must understand a scene, learn behaviors, and act in the physical world. In this talk, I’ll show a practical Physical AI workflow using OpenUSD, BowerBot, NVIDIA Isaac Sim and Isaac Lab to build a robot’s virtual world, including its body, cameras, sensors, and environment.

We’ll explore how demonstrations and reinforcement learning can teach behaviors in simulation, how vision and sensor data become observations for a robot policy, and what needs to match when transferring that behavior to real hardware. The demo follows a small robot from a simulated environment toward a real-world task, exposing both the power and the limitations of sim-to-real.

The goal is to make the path from pixels to actions concrete for computer vision and machine learning practitioners.

*About the Speaker*

[Arturo Morales Rangel](https://www.linkedin.com/in/arturo-morales-rangel) is the founder of Binary Core LLC, a Physical AI engineering company working across simulation, perception, robot learning, and deployment.

**Prompting Video-Language Models in Production: Lessons from Enterprise Video Tagging and Evaluation**

Video-language models can now describe, tag and answer questions about long-form video, but production results depend heavily on prompt design and evaluation. This talk shares field lessons from deploying such models for media, news, streaming and sports organizations, including how to structure prompts for consistent, schema-bound outputs across hours of footage.

On one sports video-tagging project, consolidating the prompt definitions cut estimated processing cost about 3x, and about 90% of the originally reported issues were later resolved through prompting alone. I'll also walk through building evaluation frameworks for video outputs, including for hard domains like egocentric video, and what changes when migrating between model versions.

Attendees will leave with reusable prompt patterns and an evaluation checklist they can apply to their own video pipelines.

*About the Speaker*

[Yash Gugale](https://www.linkedin.com/in/yashgugale/) is a Senior Forward Deployed Engineer at TwelveLabs in New York, integrating video foundation models (Marengo for embeddings and search, Pegasus for video-language understanding) for media, news, streaming and sports customers. He previously spent about six years in video streaming engineering at Peloton and Samsung TV Plus, and holds an MS in Computer Graphics Technology from Purdue.

title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians
description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority,  and is published that it may go down to posterity.”  

The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.

But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting. No extant copies could be found.

The debate over the authenticity of the Mecklenburg Declaration began. And, when a copy of a document called the Mecklenburg Resolves written on May 30, 1775, was discovered in a 1775 newspaper, the debate intensified. The Resolves were revolutionary, but stopped short of declaring independence. Did both documents exist? Or was the Declaration being conflated with the Resolves?

Examine the evidence and decide for yourself by visiting the new exhibit, “Mecklenburg Declaration?” at the Presbyterian Heritage Center.

The PHC is open Tuesday-Friday (10-4) and Saturday (12-4).

title: Carolina History Tour
description:
Learn more about the history of the nation’s first public university by attending a Carolina History Tour. The Carolina History Tours cover more than 200 years of the history of UNC-Chapel Hill, including the establishment of the university in the 18th century, the history of campus landmarks including the Old Well, Davie Poplar, and Unsung Founders Memorial, the push to open enrollment to all North Carolinians, and the growth of the school in the 20th and 21st centuries. Tours will begin at the Old Well and finish at Wilson Library. Most tours last a little over an hour. 

Led by staff from the Wilson Special Collections Library, these tours are part of the University Library’s commitment to collecting, preserving, and sharing the history of the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. 

Registration is required. You can register for your spot here.

title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians
description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority,  and is published that it may go down to posterity.”  

The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.

But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting. No extant copies could be found.

The debate over the authenticity of the Mecklenburg Declaration began. And, when a copy of a document called the Mecklenburg Resolves written on May 30, 1775, was discovered in a 1775 newspaper, the debate intensified. The Resolves were revolutionary, but stopped short of declaring independence. Did both documents exist? Or was the Declaration being conflated with the Resolves?

Examine the evidence and decide for yourself by visiting the new exhibit, “Mecklenburg Declaration?” at the Presbyterian Heritage Center.

The PHC is open Tuesday-Friday (10-4) and Saturday (12-4).

title: Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage
description: Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage at the Gregg Museum of Art & Design presents a series of vignettes exploring spaces of dignity, belonging, safety, and imagination within Black communities across North Carolina. Featuring historical photographs, contemporary images, artworks from the Gregg Museum collection including a handmade guitar by Freeman Vines, and ephemera from community partners, the exhibition reflects on place, memory, creativity, and spiritual resilience across generations. Through stories of triumph and adversity, Community Stories honors the ways Black Americans have sustained and uplifted their communities through family, entrepreneurship, cultural expression, and soulful imagination, while inspiring future generations.

title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians
description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority,  and is published that it may go down to posterity.”  

The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.

But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting. No extant copies could be found.

The debate over the authenticity of the Mecklenburg Declaration began. And, when a copy of a document called the Mecklenburg Resolves written on May 30, 1775, was discovered in a 1775 newspaper, the debate intensified. The Resolves were revolutionary, but stopped short of declaring independence. Did both documents exist? Or was the Declaration being conflated with the Resolves?

Examine the evidence and decide for yourself by visiting the new exhibit, “Mecklenburg Declaration?” at the Presbyterian Heritage Center.

The PHC is open Tuesday-Friday (10-4) and Saturday (12-4).

title: Strengthening Families Protective Factors Training
description:
Join the Positive Childhood Alliance NC on Tuesday, December 15th for a virtual introduction to the Protective Factors training. 
Protective factors are attributes that serve as buffers, helping parents find resources, supports, or coping strategies that allow them to parent effectively, even under stress. This course from Positive Childhood Alliance North Carolina helps child welfare systems, early education, prevention organizations, and other programs work with parents to build five protective factors that, when present, increase the overall well-being of children and families. 
The Five Protective Factors are the foundation to:
Enhancing parental resilience, providing an array of social connections, providing parents with concrete support, helping facilitate knowledge of parenting and child development, and supporting healthy social & emotional development in young children. 
Please note the following information:
• This is an Introductory Training.
• This training does not provide CEUs or Contact Hours.
• Participants will receive a certificate of completion and resources in your pre- and post-emails.
• Participants will not receive a copy of the PowerPoint, and the training will not be recorded.

title: Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage
description: Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage at the Gregg Museum of Art & Design presents a series of vignettes exploring spaces of dignity, belonging, safety, and imagination within Black communities across North Carolina. Featuring historical photographs, contemporary images, artworks from the Gregg Museum collection including a handmade guitar by Freeman Vines, and ephemera from community partners, the exhibition reflects on place, memory, creativity, and spiritual resilience across generations. Through stories of triumph and adversity, Community Stories honors the ways Black Americans have sustained and uplifted their communities through family, entrepreneurship, cultural expression, and soulful imagination, while inspiring future generations.

title: Digital Accessibility Pop-Up Labs
description:
The POP Lab is a drop-in workspace where UNC faculty and staff can make progress with support from digital accessibility consultants. Bring your documents, course materials, websites, reports, or questions, and work at your own pace. Come by for a few minutes or stay for the full session to ask questions, explore tools, solve problems and make meaningful progress toward expanding access.

 

Progress Over Perfection

Progress means recognizing common barriers in the platforms you use and taking small steps to reduce them. It’s choosing web formats over PDFs, applying table headers, checking color contrast and collaborating on accessible templates so everyone can start from a strong foundation. Digital accessibility depends on steady, intentional progress, not perfection, to expand access for all.

title: Bill of Rights Day Commemoration
location: Patriot Square at City Hall, Outside
description:
SAR and DAR Chapters Join Together to Honor America’s Founding Principles and New Bern’s Revolutionary Heritage During the Nation’s 250th Anniversary Year

NEW BERN, NORTH CAROLINA — On Tuesday, December 15, 2026, at 2:00 p.m., the New Bern Chapter, Sons of the American Revolution (SAR) and the Richard Dobbs Spaight Chapter of the National Society Daughters of the American Revolution (NSDAR) will present a special Bill of Rights Day commemoration and the dedication of a new granite and bronze marker honoring the historic New Bern Resolves.

The ceremony will take place at Patriot Square at City Hall, located at 300 Pollock Street in downtown New Bern.

The event brings together two important milestones in American history: the ratification of the United States Bill of Rights on December 15, 1791, and the adoption of the New Bern Resolves in August 1774, during the First Provincial Congress that was held in the then Thirteen Colonies.

The Bill of Rights: Protecting America’s Fundamental Freedoms

On December 15, 1791, the first ten amendments to the United States Constitution were ratified, becoming known as the Bill of Rights.

Originally proposed by Congress in 1789, these amendments established essential protections against government infringement of individual liberties. Among them are freedom of speech, religion, the press, peaceful assembly, and petition; protections against unreasonable searches and seizures; and important guarantees of due process and fair treatment under the law.

The 2026 commemoration marks the 235th anniversary of this historic achievement and provides an opportunity to reflect upon the enduring importance of constitutional rights and responsibilities.

The New Bern Resolves: A Defining Moment in North Carolina History

New Bern holds a significant place in America’s Revolutionary story.

On August 25, 1774, seventy-one delegates from across North Carolina assembled in New Bern for not only the “first” North Carolina Provincial Congress, but the very first Provincial Congress held in all of the Thirteen Colonies. Meeting in defiance of British royal authority, the delegates gathered to address growing grievances concerning taxation, representation, and the actions of the British government.

During the three-day gathering, delegates adopted a series of resolutions that became known as the New Bern Resolves.

These resolutions expressed opposition to British policies and affirmed the colonists’ determination to defend their rights. The Congress also selected William Hooper, Joseph Hewes, and Richard Caswell to represent North Carolina at the First Continental Congress in Philadelphia.

The New Bern Resolves became an important milestone in North Carolina’s growing resistance to British rule and helped set the stage for the American Revolution.

The commemorative event flyer features an artistic depiction of the signing of the United States Constitution, recognizing a New Bern native, Richard Dobbs Spaight’s place among the nation’s Founding Fathers.

His story provides an important historical connection between New Bern’s Revolutionary heritage, the establishment of the United States Constitution, and the fundamental liberties protected by the Bill of Rights.

Preserving History for Future Generations

A highlight of the December 15th ceremony will be the formal dedication of the new New Bern Resolves Granite & Bronze Marker at Patriot Square.

The marker will serve as a lasting reminder of New Bern’s contribution to the founding of our nation and provide residents and visitors with an opportunity to learn about this significant chapter of American history.

The ceremony will also feature a presentation on the history and importance of the Bill of Rights, along with live musket volleys by the New Bern Chapter SAR Musket Cadre.

Honoring America’s 250th Anniversary

As the United States commemorates the 250th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence in 2026, the ceremony offers a meaningful opportunity to recognize the individuals and events that shaped the nation’s founding.

By connecting New Bern’s Revolutionary history with the constitutional protections established through the Bill of Rights, the event highlights the continuing importance of understanding, preserving, and sharing America’s history.

The New Bern Chapter, Sons of the American Revolution and the Richard Dobbs Spaight Chapter NSDAR invite the community to join them for this historic occasion.

Gary Gillette, President of the New Bern Chapter, Sons of the American Revolution said

“I welcome and encourage everyone to join us for the historic occasion. It’s an opportunity for everyone to not only to help celebrate the events that occurred, but to also learn a bit more about our nation’s history, and how our small town of New Bern played such a key role in its history.”

Tammy Gillette, Regent of the Richard Dobbs Spaight NSDAR Chapter said “that the commemoration of the Bill of Rights and the dedication of the New Bern Resolves Plaque reminds us that the liberties we cherish today were secured through the courage and sacrifice of those who came before us. As we gather to honor these historic milestones, we celebrate not only our nation's founding principles but also New Bern's unique place in the story of our American freedom. It is our responsibility to preserve this legacy and inspire future generations to uphold the rights and responsibilities of what our forefathers fought for."

Event Information

Event: U.S. Bill of Rights Day Commemoration and New Bern Resolves Granite & Bronze Marker Dedication

Date: Tuesday, December 15, 2026

Time: 2:00 p.m.

Location: Patriot Square at City Hall, 300 Pollock Street, New Bern, North Carolina

Presented by: New Bern Chapter, Sons of the American Revolution and the Richard Dobbs Spaight Chapter NSDAR

Program Highlights: Bill of Rights historical presentation, dedication of the New Bern Resolves Granite & Bronze Marker, and ceremonial musket volleys by the New Bern Chapter SAR Musket Cadre.  Refreshments served afterwards.

This sub-group focuses on Speculative Fiction, including Science Fiction, Fantasy and Horror. If you have anything that falls under that category — be it short story, poem, novel-in-progress or screenplay — then come! We'd love to hear from you.

Our format allows each reader 15 minutes to present their work aloud, followed by approximately 20 minutes of feedback from the other attendees. To ensure fairness, each attendee is limited to 1 minute of Initial Feedback time. During that period, the author remains silent. Next, we have a 5 minute Free-For-All discussion about the work -- then the author may speak. (We usually get through three readers.)

Though not required, in order to receive more in-depth feed-back, readers may post their work in advance on our Google Group:
https://groups.google.com/d/forum/durham-sff-writers-group

We ask that participants keep their comments constructive and respectful, focusing on what works or doesn't work in the piece.

We also ask that readers provide a warning, both on the Google Group and during the meeting, if their story features content that some readers might find upsetting. This includes descriptions of violence or sexual content.

title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians
description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority,  and is published that it may go down to posterity.”  

The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.

But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting. No extant copies could be found.

The debate over the authenticity of the Mecklenburg Declaration began. And, when a copy of a document called the Mecklenburg Resolves written on May 30, 1775, was discovered in a 1775 newspaper, the debate intensified. The Resolves were revolutionary, but stopped short of declaring independence. Did both documents exist? Or was the Declaration being conflated with the Resolves?

Examine the evidence and decide for yourself by visiting the new exhibit, “Mecklenburg Declaration?” at the Presbyterian Heritage Center.

The PHC is open Tuesday-Friday (10-4) and Saturday (12-4).

title: Team ENOUGH Welcome Session (For Young People Under 26)
description:
Link to join: https://www.mobilize.us/join/46980109/1:6745cbfdda64f3037e6e93179c06aad9a1b686584ec21dddb065a4e30d642e4f/

How to join:
Please join our virtual welcome session with this link

Are you a young person between 13 and 25 years old who is interested in taking action around preventing gun violence? Join us for our Team ENOUGH welcome session to learn more about the different ways you can engage. 

Team ENOUGH is a youth-led program whose mission is to educate young voices about gun violence and mobilize them to take meaningful action against it. Supported by Brady United, we harness the expertise and experience of today’s youth to advance our intersectional work across the country. 

Led by an Executive Council, comprised of students just like us, we believe that diversity is a strength, and that only when everyone has a seat at the table can we build an effective movement to prevent all gun violence in all communities.

For us, preventing gun violence not only requires regulating access to firearms but also addressing how systemic racism and environmental factors cause this form of bloodshed to run especially rampant in communities of color. You cannot talk about gun violence without talking about police brutality, white supremacy, the broken criminal justice system, poverty, homophobia, access to affordable housing, or the often barriers separating disadvantaged populations from physical and mental healthcare. 

So if you share this belief, join us for our Team ENOUGH welcome session and become part of the movement to end gun violence in our lifetime.

title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians
description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority,  and is published that it may go down to posterity.”  

The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.

But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting. No extant copies could be found.

The debate over the authenticity of the Mecklenburg Declaration began. And, when a copy of a document called the Mecklenburg Resolves written on May 30, 1775, was discovered in a 1775 newspaper, the debate intensified. The Resolves were revolutionary, but stopped short of declaring independence. Did both documents exist? Or was the Declaration being conflated with the Resolves?

Examine the evidence and decide for yourself by visiting the new exhibit, “Mecklenburg Declaration?” at the Presbyterian Heritage Center.

The PHC is open Tuesday-Friday (10-4) and Saturday (12-4).

title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians
description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority,  and is published that it may go down to posterity.”  

The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.

But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting. No extant copies could be found.

The debate over the authenticity of the Mecklenburg Declaration began. And, when a copy of a document called the Mecklenburg Resolves written on May 30, 1775, was discovered in a 1775 newspaper, the debate intensified. The Resolves were revolutionary, but stopped short of declaring independence. Did both documents exist? Or was the Declaration being conflated with the Resolves?

Examine the evidence and decide for yourself by visiting the new exhibit, “Mecklenburg Declaration?” at the Presbyterian Heritage Center.

The PHC is open Tuesday-Friday (10-4) and Saturday (12-4).

title: Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage
description: Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage at the Gregg Museum of Art & Design presents a series of vignettes exploring spaces of dignity, belonging, safety, and imagination within Black communities across North Carolina. Featuring historical photographs, contemporary images, artworks from the Gregg Museum collection including a handmade guitar by Freeman Vines, and ephemera from community partners, the exhibition reflects on place, memory, creativity, and spiritual resilience across generations. Through stories of triumph and adversity, Community Stories honors the ways Black Americans have sustained and uplifted their communities through family, entrepreneurship, cultural expression, and soulful imagination, while inspiring future generations.

title: Tour of Coker Aboretum
location: Coker Arboretum, 399 E. Cameron Avenue, Chapel Hill, NC, 27514, United States
description:
with Geoffrey Neal, Curator, Coker Arboretum 
  
Discover this five-acre gem in the heart of the UNC campus! Established in 1903, Coker Arboretum is part of the North Carolina Botanical Garden and features a diverse collection of plants, including flowering trees and shrubs, bulbs, and perennials. Join a Coker Arboretum curator for a winter walking tour and explore the history and beauty of this beloved garden. 
Offered each season, every tour reveals something new as the Coker Arboretum changes throughout the year. 
  
Register here!
  
Accessibility:  
This is an outdoor tour that follows mostly flat pathways, including brick and smooth or compacted grit surfaces.  After rains, grit paths may become uneven, eroded, or soggy, which may affect ease of travel. Participants are welcome to move at their own pace and take breaks as needed. We’ll be happy to discuss your needs and determine how we can best support your participation.

title: Winter Solstice Bird Walk
location: Brumley North Nature Preserve, 3620 Old State Highway 10, Chapel Hill, NC, 27514, United States
description:
Welcome the winter season with the birds of Brumley North!
Cross the bridge into winter as evening birding peaks at Brumley North at the exact moment the winter solstice occurs! Back by popular demand, the winter solstice bird walk led by TLC Trail Guide, Patrick D, will unite patrons of the Tri-County Conservationists chapter of the North Carolina Wildlife Federation with TLC supporters in its second year in a row!

White-throated sparrows, eastern bluebirds, Carolina wrens, and more avian residents of the preserve will sound off the transition from autumn to winter as the shortest day of the year comes to a close and the longest night of the year begins. Hikers will be invited to ground themselves at TLC's Healing Labyrinth and admire its American Beautyberries, known to attract hermit thrushes and other birds. You will then be led through the pines of Cemetery Connector Trail out to the bridge to complete Dairy Farm Trail, then return back the way we came. This is a free event, but preregistration is required.



Quick Details:

 	Hike Leader: Patrick D., TLC Trail Guide

 	Distance & Speed: 1.3 miles, slow pace
 	Age Group: 12 and older
 	Extras: Bring binoculars, comfortable warm clothes, and flashlights, as our hike will conclude in the dusk!

title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians
description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority,  and is published that it may go down to posterity.”  

The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.

But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting. No extant copies could be found.

The debate over the authenticity of the Mecklenburg Declaration began. And, when a copy of a document called the Mecklenburg Resolves written on May 30, 1775, was discovered in a 1775 newspaper, the debate intensified. The Resolves were revolutionary, but stopped short of declaring independence. Did both documents exist? Or was the Declaration being conflated with the Resolves?

Examine the evidence and decide for yourself by visiting the new exhibit, “Mecklenburg Declaration?” at the Presbyterian Heritage Center.

The PHC is open Tuesday-Friday (10-4) and Saturday (12-4).

title: Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage
description: Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage at the Gregg Museum of Art & Design presents a series of vignettes exploring spaces of dignity, belonging, safety, and imagination within Black communities across North Carolina. Featuring historical photographs, contemporary images, artworks from the Gregg Museum collection including a handmade guitar by Freeman Vines, and ephemera from community partners, the exhibition reflects on place, memory, creativity, and spiritual resilience across generations. Through stories of triumph and adversity, Community Stories honors the ways Black Americans have sustained and uplifted their communities through family, entrepreneurship, cultural expression, and soulful imagination, while inspiring future generations.

title: Goldston America 250 Film Series
description:
Join the Chatham Community Library for this Goldston America 250 Film Series, hosted every fourth Tuesday, January-December 2026, 4pm-6pm. America 250’s mission is to honor and commemorate the 250th anniversary of the signing of the Declaration of Independence, marking America’s Semiquincentennial. The Goldston Library will screen the following documentaries and films:

Tue, Jan 27, 4pm-6pm The Congress, Ken Burns.
Tue, Feb 24, 4pm-6pm Becoming Frederick Douglass, Stanley Nelson and Nicole London.
Tue, Mar 24, 4pm-6pm Rachel Carson: The Woman Who Launched the Modern Environmental Movement, Michelle Ferrari.
Tue, Apr 28, 4pm-6pm Thomas Jefferson: A View from the Mountain, Martin Doblmeier.
Tue, May 26, 4pm-6pm The Address, Ken Burns.
Tue, Jun 23, 4pm-6pm The Brooklyn Bridge, Ken Burns.
Tue, Jul 28, 4pm-6pm The Statue of Liberty, Ken Burns.
Tue, Aug 25, 4pm-6pm American Coup: Wilmington 1898, Yoruba Richen and Brad Lichtenstein.
Tue, Sep 22, 4pm-6pm How it Feels to be Free, Yoruba Richen.
Tue, Oct 27, 4pm-6pm 80 Years Later, Celine Parreñas Shimizu.
Tue, Nov 24, 4pm-6pm Gather, Sanjay Rawal.
Tue, Dec 22, 4pm-6pm Women of World War II: The Untold Stories, Eli Brown.

This FREE, family-friendly event is open to the public. No registration is required. The event will take place indoors in the Goldston Library. The Goldston Library is ADA-compliant, including wheelchair-accessible parking, entrances, seating, common spaces, walkways, and restrooms. Free parking is available outside the library. Pets are not allowed - please leave your furry friends at home.

This event is part of our Chatham Celebrates America 250 initiative. See more America 250 events.

title: DCABP monthly meeting
description: Durham Committee on the Affairs of Black People (DCABP) - Political Action Committee. title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians
description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority,  and is published that it may go down to posterity.”  

The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.

But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting. No extant copies could be found.

The debate over the authenticity of the Mecklenburg Declaration began. And, when a copy of a document called the Mecklenburg Resolves written on May 30, 1775, was discovered in a 1775 newspaper, the debate intensified. The Resolves were revolutionary, but stopped short of declaring independence. Did both documents exist? Or was the Declaration being conflated with the Resolves?

Examine the evidence and decide for yourself by visiting the new exhibit, “Mecklenburg Declaration?” at the Presbyterian Heritage Center.

description:
Link to join: https://www.mobilize.us/join/46980110/1:9816963e8aaa2e7241c566f0013fea2f325f40ad57607cde0a97c11de598b340/

How to join:
Please join our virtual welcome session with this link

Are you a young person between 13 and 25 years old who is interested in taking action around preventing gun violence? Join us for our Team ENOUGH welcome session to learn more about the different ways you can engage. 

Team ENOUGH is a youth-led program whose mission is to educate young voices about gun violence and mobilize them to take meaningful action against it. Supported by Brady United, we harness the expertise and experience of today’s youth to advance our intersectional work across the country. 

Led by an Executive Council, comprised of students just like us, we believe that diversity is a strength, and that only when everyone has a seat at the table can we build an effective movement to prevent all gun violence in all communities.

For us, preventing gun violence not only requires regulating access to firearms but also addressing how systemic racism and environmental factors cause this form of bloodshed to run especially rampant in communities of color. You cannot talk about gun violence without talking about police brutality, white supremacy, the broken criminal justice system, poverty, homophobia, access to affordable housing, or the often barriers separating disadvantaged populations from physical and mental healthcare. 

So if you share this belief, join us for our Team ENOUGH welcome session and become part of the movement to end gun violence in our lifetime.

How to prepare:
We are excited to see you soon!

P.S. This is a call for young people from 13-25 years old who are interested in getting engaged with the Team ENOUGH program. If you are over the age of 25 please sign up for the Brady Welcome Session at https://www.mobilize.us/brady/event/274016/

Thank you for signing up! Here are some notes before the phone bank.

title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians
description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority,  and is published that it may go down to posterity.”  

The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.

But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting. No extant copies could be found.

The debate over the authenticity of the Mecklenburg Declaration began. And, when a copy of a document called the Mecklenburg Resolves written on May 30, 1775, was discovered in a 1775 newspaper, the debate intensified. The Resolves were revolutionary, but stopped short of declaring independence. Did both documents exist? Or was the Declaration being conflated with the Resolves?

Examine the evidence and decide for yourself by visiting the new exhibit, “Mecklenburg Declaration?” at the Presbyterian Heritage Center.

The PHC is open Tuesday-Friday (10-4) and Saturday (12-4).

title: Hip Hop Nutcracker
location: Durham Performing Arts Center (DPAC), 123 Vivian Street / William V. 'Bill' Bell Way, Durham, NC, 27701, United States
description:
A holiday mash-up for the whole family, The Hip Hop Nutcracker returns for another spectacular tour. Directed and choreographed by Tony and Olivier Award-nominated Jennifer Weber, this contemporary dance spectacle is a re-mixed and re-imagined version of the classic, smashing hip hop dance and Tchaikovsky’s timeless music together into a heart-stirring and inspirational holiday event. The Hip Hop Nutcracker is brought to life by a powerhouse cast of a dozen all-star dancers, a DJ, a violinist, and MC Kurtis Blow, one of hip hop’s founding fathers, who opens the show with a short set.

Just like the original, in The Hip Hop Nutcracker, Maria-Clara and the Nutcracker Prince go on a dream adventure battling a gang of mice, visiting the land of sweets and learning the lessons of the holiday season. Innovative digital graffiti and visuals transform the landscape of E.T.A. Hoffmann’s beloved story from traditional 19th Century Germany to the vibrant, diverse sights and sounds of contemporary New York City.

Grab your family and friends and let the dynamic performers of The Hip Hop Nutcracker take you on a journey that celebrates love, community and the magic of the holiday season. Get your tickets here!

title: *IN-PERSON* SF/F Group
description:
Durham Writers Group
We will be at the Moon House at 3039 University Dr. in Durham. This venue does not serve food or drink, but feel free to bring your own. There is a kitchenette for our use, but be sure to clean up afterwards. The space might be a little cozy; please consider masking or staying home if you have a respiratory ailment.

This sub-group focuses on Speculative Fiction, including Science Fiction, Fantasy and Horror. If you have anything that falls under that category — be it short story, poem, novel-in-progress or screenplay — then come! We'd love to hear from you.

Our format allows each reader 15 minutes to present their work aloud, followed by approximately 20 minutes of feedback from the other attendees. To ensure fairness, each attendee is limited to 1 minute of Initial Feedback time. During that period, the author remains silent. Next, we have a 5 minute Free-For-All discussion about the work -- then the author may speak. (We usually get through three readers.)

Though not required, in order to receive more in-depth feed-back, readers may post their work in advance on our Google Group:
https://groups.google.com/d/forum/durham-sff-writers-group

We ask that participants keep their comments constructive and respectful, focusing on what works or doesn't work in the piece.

We also ask that readers provide a warning, both on the Google Group and during the meeting, if their story features content that some readers might find upsetting. This includes descriptions of violence or sexual content.
