title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians
description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority,  and is published that it may go down to posterity.”  

The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.

But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting. No extant copies could be found.

The debate over the authenticity of the Mecklenburg Declaration began. And, when a copy of a document called the Mecklenburg Resolves written on May 30, 1775, was discovered in a 1775 newspaper, the debate intensified. The Resolves were revolutionary, but stopped short of declaring independence. Did both documents exist? Or was the Declaration being conflated with the Resolves?

Examine the evidence and decide for yourself by visiting the new exhibit, “Mecklenburg Declaration?” at the Presbyterian Heritage Center.

The PHC is open Tuesday-Friday (10-4) and Saturday (12-4).

title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians
description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority,  and is published that it may go down to posterity.”  

The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.

But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting. No extant copies could be found.

The debate over the authenticity of the Mecklenburg Declaration began. And, when a copy of a document called the Mecklenburg Resolves written on May 30, 1775, was discovered in a 1775 newspaper, the debate intensified. The Resolves were revolutionary, but stopped short of declaring independence. Did both documents exist? Or was the Declaration being conflated with the Resolves?

Examine the evidence and decide for yourself by visiting the new exhibit, “Mecklenburg Declaration?” at the Presbyterian Heritage Center.

The PHC is open Tuesday-Friday (10-4) and Saturday (12-4).

title: Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage
description: Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage at the Gregg Museum of Art & Design presents a series of vignettes exploring spaces of dignity, belonging, safety, and imagination within Black communities across North Carolina. Featuring historical photographs, contemporary images, artworks from the Gregg Museum collection including a handmade guitar by Freeman Vines, and ephemera from community partners, the exhibition reflects on place, memory, creativity, and spiritual resilience across generations. Through stories of triumph and adversity, Community Stories honors the ways Black Americans have sustained and uplifted their communities through family, entrepreneurship, cultural expression, and soulful imagination, while inspiring future generations.

title: Applications Open: TEDxChavisWay Youth
location: John Chavis Memorial Community Center, 505 Martin Luther King Jr Blvd, Raleigh, NC, 27601, United States
description:
Applications are open for TEDxChavisWay Youth, an independently organized TED event happening on May 1, 2027 at the John Chavis Memorial Community Center in Raleigh. Youth between the ages of 10 and 19 who may be interested in speaking or performing at the event are encouraged to apply by the deadline, January 4th. The full application link can be found here. 
TEDxChavisWay Youth is curated by a team of volunteers in partnership with NC State Extension program #PassTheMicYouth, Wake County 4-H, and Raleigh Parks and Recreation. Their goal is to bring together bright young minds to give talks that are idea-focused to foster learning, inspiration and wonder—and provoke conversations that matter. 
Talks will be filmed and edited and videos will be hosted on the TEDx YouTube channel. All speakers will be assigned a coach to guide them through the process of crafting a talk, from script to stage. Talks should be at or around 5 minutes on any topic related to the theme Speak Up, Speak Out, which celebrates young visionaries, storytellers, and changemakers who are shaping the world through the power of their voices and ideas. (Note: The theme is open to each individual’s interpretation). Performances can be up to 5 minutes and can include original music, spoken word poetry, dance, and other forms of artistic expression.

title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians
description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority,  and is published that it may go down to posterity.”  

The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.

But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting. No extant copies could be found.

The debate over the authenticity of the Mecklenburg Declaration began. And, when a copy of a document called the Mecklenburg Resolves written on May 30, 1775, was discovered in a 1775 newspaper, the debate intensified. The Resolves were revolutionary, but stopped short of declaring independence. Did both documents exist? Or was the Declaration being conflated with the Resolves?

Examine the evidence and decide for yourself by visiting the new exhibit, “Mecklenburg Declaration?” at the Presbyterian Heritage Center.

The PHC is open Tuesday-Friday (10-4) and Saturday (12-4).

How to join:
Thank you for signing up! Here are some notes before the phone bank.

This phone bank will be easier if you are **not doing everything on your phone or tablet**, we recommend you use two devices, preferably a phone and a computer, and we highly recommend you join us at home or in a quiet area. 

We will be using Scale to Win to make calls.

Join Common Cause for an important phone bank as we mobilize voters to take action against dangerous legislation in state houses around the country. We will focus on the most urgent campaigns that need our help. Some of these campaigns may include stopping bills that will make it harder for millions of Americans—especially students, seniors, and veterans—to cast their ballots. We need your help to ensure voters across the country call their state representatives and demand they protect the freedom to vote.

No prior experience is necessary—our team will provide full training at the start of each shift!

## What to Expect:

* A step-by-step walkthrough of our Phone Dialer tools.
* Expert tips on effective communication with voters.
* Opportunities to ask questions and connect with other like-minded volunteers.


Sign up today and take the first step toward empowering voters and protecting democracy in 2025!

title: “To BEethoven Rather Than To Seem”: Part III | Gut Instinct Chamber Music Project
description:
FEATURING

Nicholas DiEguenio, violin
Mimi Solomon, piano

 

PROGRAM

Featuring Beethoven’s heroic and youthful Violin Sonata No. 3 and the Jesse Jones Scherzo it inspired

This season, Gut Instinct takes on the large-scale project “To Beethoven Rather Than To Seem,” marking 200 years since Beethoven’s death and 250 since the U.S. Declaration of Independence. Over the course of five concerts, Nicholas DiEugenio and pianist Mimi Solomon will present all ten Beethoven Sonatas on period instruments along with five commissioned works written expressly for them.

 

PARKING

Please plan to arrive early as parking on campus can be tricky. Learn more about parking and directions to UNC-Chapel Hill’s campus.

 

The Gut Instinct Chamber Music Project, now in its third season, is a concert series in the Triangle area which brings UNC-Chapel Hill and Duke University’s historical instrument collections together with artists committed to presenting inspired, visceral, historically informed performances of the 19th-century chamber music repertoire. The series features music of female composers and their artistic circles. The name “Gut Instinct” is a play on words. In 19th-century Europe, the violin, viola, and cello were strung with (sheep) gut.

 

All of the artists collaborating with the Pleyel and Graf pianos at UNC-Chapel Hill (built in 19th-century Paris and Vienna, respectively), as well as the Clementi piano at Duke (early 19th-century England) use these gut string materials. The turn of phrase “gut instinct” also refers to the visceral, accessible nature of the musical performances that this series presents. Our mission is to make “Historically Informed Performance” accessible, relatable, and culturally relevant! We also want to feature these special pianos that are rarely heard by the public, along with great music by female composers which has remained lesser known to the greater public for far too long, and living composers who are keeping our art form alive!

title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians
description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority,  and is published that it may go down to posterity.”  

The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.

But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting. No extant copies could be found.

The debate over the authenticity of the Mecklenburg Declaration began. And, when a copy of a document called the Mecklenburg Resolves written on May 30, 1775, was discovered in a 1775 newspaper, the debate intensified. The Resolves were revolutionary, but stopped short of declaring independence. Did both documents exist? Or was the Declaration being conflated with the Resolves?

Examine the evidence and decide for yourself by visiting the new exhibit, “Mecklenburg Declaration?” at the Presbyterian Heritage Center.

The PHC is open Tuesday-Friday (10-4) and Saturday (12-4).

title: Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage
description: Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage at the Gregg Museum of Art & Design presents a series of vignettes exploring spaces of dignity, belonging, safety, and imagination within Black communities across North Carolina. Featuring historical photographs, contemporary images, artworks from the Gregg Museum collection including a handmade guitar by Freeman Vines, and ephemera from community partners, the exhibition reflects on place, memory, creativity, and spiritual resilience across generations. Through stories of triumph and adversity, Community Stories honors the ways Black Americans have sustained and uplifted their communities through family, entrepreneurship, cultural expression, and soulful imagination, while inspiring future generations.

title: Durham Social Hack Night
description:
Triangle Developers
Hey tech folks, come out and hang at Hi-Wire starting at 6pm! Hack Night is meant to be a social evening for folks in tech. It's less about networking and more about community.

**Look for the Hack Night tabletop sign** and nerds wearing name tags to find us. If the weather is nice, we'll probably be outside.

Help folks feel welcome by using the **"Pac Man Rule"** \- when standing with a group of people \(usually in a circle\)\, leave some space open so that another person can easily join\.

See our [Code of Conduct](https://github.com/TriangleDevsSlack/policies/blob/master/code-of-conduct.md). To summarize: be nice or leave. No tolerance for harassment or oppression. In addition, since alcohol is present at these events, please be mindful of your consumption and respect other people's choices on whether or not to consume.

**FAQs**
*Do folks hack at Hack Night? Should I bring my computer?*
This is more of a night for hackers than an actual hack night. You're welcome to bring a laptop, but most people will only be socializing.

*What are the beverage options? Are there any non-alcoholic drinks?*
Hi-Wire Brewing offers many types of beers including a few non-alcoholic options plus wine and some liquor. They usually have a happy hour special on the first few beers on the menu. In the same complex are Cugino Forno which has additional drink options, and Two Roosters which has excellent ice cream.

*Are there any drink specials?*
If Hack Night is on a Tuesday, Hi-Wire usually has $5 pints for their flagship beers. Look for the list at the counter.

*Do people eat snacks/dinner during the meetup?*
Sometimes folks will order a pizza or salad from Cugino Forno. I sometimes grab an ice cream from Two Roosters across the way. Most people eat before or after but it's no big deal - whatever you prefer and are most comfortable with.

*How can I connect with the developer community?*
Go to [triangledevelopers.com](https://triangledevelopers.com/) to find the Discord and Slack info.

title: Sold Out: Mexico’s Magical Migrations Institute
location: Toluca, Macho de Agua, and Puerto Vallarta, Mexico and Raleigh, N.C.
description:
Applications for the 2027 Mexico’s Magical Migrations Institute are now closed. 

Experience one of the world’s greatest migrations: monarch butterflies on their wintering grounds.Observe humpback whale social interactions.Visit and learn about the Mazahua people at La Casa de la Cultura Mazahua.Discover connections between Mexico and North Carolina.Participating educators will witness two of nature’s greatest spectacles – wintering monarch butterflies and humpback whales. Each year one of the world’s greatest migrations takes place as millions of monarch butterflies from the US and Canada travel south to the forested Mexican highlands. Once they arrive, they begin a period of winter hibernation by clustering together in huge numbers, blanketing the surrounding vegetation. As the butterflies are arriving in Mexico, so are humpback whales. Concluding their own incredible migration from their feeding waters off Alaska, large numbers of humpback whales gather off Mexico’s Pacific coast. They come to these warmer waters to breed and to give birth. Learn about these magical migrations from local experts and explore connections to North Carolina. We will share our adventures with students at home through daily blog posts from the field.

title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians
description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority,  and is published that it may go down to posterity.”  

The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.

But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting. No extant copies could be found.

The debate over the authenticity of the Mecklenburg Declaration began. And, when a copy of a document called the Mecklenburg Resolves written on May 30, 1775, was discovered in a 1775 newspaper, the debate intensified. The Resolves were revolutionary, but stopped short of declaring independence. Did both documents exist? Or was the Declaration being conflated with the Resolves?

Examine the evidence and decide for yourself by visiting the new exhibit, “Mecklenburg Declaration?” at the Presbyterian Heritage Center.

The PHC is open Tuesday-Friday (10-4) and Saturday (12-4).

title: Jan 14 - MCP, Agents and Skills Meetup
description:
Raleigh AI, Machine Learning and Computer Vision Meetup
Join our virtual meetup to hear talks from experts on cutting-edge topics across AI, ML, and computer vision.

**Date, Time and Location**

Jan 14, 2027
9:00 AM - 11:00 AM PST
Online. **[Register for the Zoom!](https://voxel51.com/events/mcp-agents-skills-meetup-january-14-2027)**

**From Demo to Production: Testing, Scaling and Securing AI Agents with Spring AI**

Your agent works perfectly in the demo. Then in production it gives a wrong answer and nobody can tell why, token costs spike, it slows to a crawl under load, and it calls a tool the user was never allowed to use. Building an agent is the easy part; the real work is running it like any other production service: tested, observable, scalable and secure.

Spring AI lets you do that with the Spring idioms and tooling you already know. This code-first session grows one example step by step. We start with a simple ChatClient, add advisors, memory and RAG, comparing the options Spring AI offers for each, and then let the agent act through tool calling and MCP.

Then come the production questions:

* Testing: we catch regressions with LLM-as-judge evaluators and typed decision models like Jev for fast, cheap verdicts.
* Observability: we add Micrometer traces, logs and token usage across model and tool calls.
* Scaling: we compare options for handling more concurrent users, from self-hosting to a managed runtime such as Amazon Bedrock AgentCore.
* Security: we use Spring Security to authenticate users and make sure only the MCP tools they're allowed to use ever get called. You'll leave with reusable Spring patterns for agents that reason and act, and the discipline to test, observe, scale and secure them in production.

*About the Speaker*

[Andrei Shakirin](https://www.linkedin.com/in/andrei-shakirin/) is a Solutions Architect at Amazon Web Services and a former Pivotal Labs engineer, specializing in the design of highly scalable systems and generative AI applications. He is an active committer to several Spring and Apache open-source projects, contributor into MCP java SDK and a regular speaker at technical conferences.

**From Model Evals to System Evals: Evaluating Agents, Harnesses, and the Evaluators Themselves**

Every team shipping agents is quietly standing up two systems: the agent harness that plans, retrieves, calls tools, and edits code — and the evaluation harness that decides whether any of it can be trusted. Most teams only evaluate the first one's final output.

That is not enough. An agent can produce a correct answer through an unreliable, wasteful, or out-of-policy execution path, and outcome-only checks will pass it. This talk argues for evaluating the whole agent system: execution trajectories — tool correctness, evidence and grounding, state handling, policy compliance, and efficiency — alongside final outcomes, using deterministic specification checks an agent cannot game, model-based judges, and human-calibrated benchmarks.

We separate capability evaluations from regression evaluations so harness or model changes can be gated in CI. Then we turn the lens around: the evaluators themselves need evaluating — LLM judge calibration, disagreement analysis, and where human review still belongs.

Attendees leave with a production checklist for gating agent, model, and harness changes on system-level evidence instead of final answers.

*About the Speaker*

[Dipen Chawla](https://www.linkedin.com/in/dipen-chawla-bb4a49bb/) is an AI engineer and researcher working on agentic AI systems and their evaluation, including agent memory and clinical diagnostic reasoning work at Microsoft, and data platform engineering at Walmart and S&P Global.

**Leading an Army of AI Agents**

Our AI coding agents now pick up tasks, follow team playbooks, open pull requests and wait for review. This firsthand engineering case study follows more than ten agents running in parallel and shows how briefs, shared context and verification loops keep their work reviewable.
It covers the failure modes too: confident wrong turns, incomplete verification, review bottlenecks and the attention required from human leaders.
Attendees will learn a practical task-to-PR workflow, how to make trust conditional on evidence, and which measures expose the costs hidden by faster output. The focus is on agent workflow and operating discipline, with concrete engineering examples rather than a product pitch.

*About the Speaker*

[John Adib](https://www.linkedin.com/in/MrAdib) is a London-based engineering manager at Zapp, a former CTO and two-time founder with 18+ years of software experience.

Agents in Action: Putting AI Agents to Work on Visual AI Data

What should an AI agent remember, and what should it forget? In this talk, we’ll explore the Voxel51 agent through the lens of memory, examining how retaining the right context and incorporating feedback can help agents improve over time. Through examples from visual AI workflows, we’ll discuss what’s worth remembering, from dataset context and user preferences to corrections and successful approaches, and when to update or discard information that becomes outdated. We’ll also explore how feedback and evaluation can help us determine whether an agent is making better decisions, offering practical insights for building agents that become more useful with experience.

*About the Speaker*

[Adonai Vera](https://www.linkedin.com/in/adonai-vera/) is a Machine Learning Engineer and DevRel at Voxel51 with over 7 years of experience building computer vision and machine learning models using TensorFlow, Docker, and OpenCV.

title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians
description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority,  and is published that it may go down to posterity.”  

The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.

But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting. No extant copies could be found.

The debate over the authenticity of the Mecklenburg Declaration began. And, when a copy of a document called the Mecklenburg Resolves written on May 30, 1775, was discovered in a 1775 newspaper, the debate intensified. The Resolves were revolutionary, but stopped short of declaring independence. Did both documents exist? Or was the Declaration being conflated with the Resolves?

Examine the evidence and decide for yourself by visiting the new exhibit, “Mecklenburg Declaration?” at the Presbyterian Heritage Center.

The PHC is open Tuesday-Friday (10-4) and Saturday (12-4).

title: NC Public Librarian Certification Commission
description:
The NC Public Librarian Certification Commission was formed in 1936 to set minimum standards for public librarians to protect and maintain public library resources, to assure professional management and administration of library services, to meet the personnel requirements for State Aid administered by the Library of NC, and to guarantee the best possible public library service to all North Carolinians.

The North Carolina General Statute 143B-68 states that the commission must be comprised of: the Chairman of the public libraries section of NCLA, two individuals named by the Governor upon nomination of the NCLA, the dean of a State or regionally accredited graduate school of librarianship in North Carolina appointed by the Governor, and one member at large appointed by the Governor. Commission members appointed by the Governor serve 4-year terms, all others serve 2-year terms.

Commission meetings are held quarterly to review applications and discuss Certification policies and procedures.

The commission's meeting dates for the 2025-2026 year are October 27, 2025, January 9, 2026, April 10, 2026, and July 10, 2026. All meetings are held at the Library of NC beginning at 1:00 pm unless otherwise posted. Information about meetings can be found on the North Carolina Secretary of State's meeting calendar.

Have questions about certification? Contact us at NC.Certification.Commission@dncr.nc.gov.

title: earspace | CMM 26-27
description:
FEATURING

earspace

earspace is an ensemble consisting of violin, viola, cello, flute, oboe, clarinet, piano, and percussion that performs a combination of conducted and unconducted chamber music of a wide variety of scopes. Passionate producers, the ensemble is dedicated to both commissioning new, immersive works and amplifying rarely-performed gems of the repertoire. Founded in North Carolina, the group is now based across the US and performs regularly around the east coast, collaborating with organizations including the Southern Exposure New Music Series, Towson University, Duke University, UNC Chapel Hill, the Peabody Institute, Asheville Ballet, Carolina Performing Arts, and others.

The ensemble seeks to expose the inherent potentials within every moment and space, cultivating visceral reactions unique to every manifestation. Through their projects, they explore the extremities of contemporary performance and work to bring audiences closer to the music they experience.

description:

Once they arrive, they begin a period of winter hibernation by clustering together in huge numbers, blanketing the surrounding vegetation. As the butterflies are arriving in Mexico, so are humpback whales. title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians
description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority,  and is published that it may go down to posterity.”  

The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.

But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting. No extant copies could be found.

The debate over the authenticity of the Mecklenburg Declaration began. And, when a copy of a document called the Mecklenburg Resolves written on May 30, 1775, was discovered in a 1775 newspaper, the debate intensified. The Resolves were revolutionary, but stopped short of declaring independence. Did both documents exist? Or was the Declaration being conflated with the Resolves?

Examine the evidence and decide for yourself by visiting the new exhibit, “Mecklenburg Declaration?” at the Presbyterian Heritage Center.

The PHC is open Tuesday-Friday (10-4) and Saturday (12-4).

title: Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage
description: Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage at the Gregg Museum of Art & Design presents a series of vignettes exploring spaces of dignity, belonging, safety, and imagination within Black communities across North Carolina. Featuring historical photographs, contemporary images, artworks from the Gregg Museum collection including a handmade guitar by Freeman Vines, and ephemera from community partners, the exhibition reflects on place, memory, creativity, and spiritual resilience across generations. Through stories of triumph and adversity, Community Stories honors the ways Black Americans have sustained and uplifted their communities through family, entrepreneurship, cultural expression, and soulful imagination, while inspiring future generations.

location: Witherspoon Student Center, African American Cultural Center (218)
description: Join the African American Cultural Center to experience ariana Farquharson's You Are Here: Geolocating the Self through the Familiar in the Midst of the Unfamiliar. It will be on display in the art gallery at the African American Cultural Center from Oct. 28, 2026, to  Feb. 28, 2027. A behind-the-scenes look at the exhibition is set for Nov. 11.

How to join:
Thank you for signing up! Here are some notes before the phone bank.

This phone bank will be easier if you are **not doing everything on your phone or tablet**, we recommend you use two devices, preferably a phone and a computer, and we highly recommend you join us at home or in a quiet area. 

We will be using Scale to Win to make calls. 

**Please click this link and [watch a quick training on how to use Scale to Win](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cMqsfqpHPvU).**

Join Common Cause for an important phone bank as we mobilize voters to take action against dangerous legislation in state houses around the country. We will focus on the most urgent campaigns that need our help. Some of these campaigns may include stopping bills that will make it harder for millions of Americans—especially students, seniors, and veterans—to cast their ballots. We need your help to ensure voters across the country call their state representatives and demand they protect the freedom to vote.

No prior experience is necessary—our team will provide full training at the start of each shift!

## What to Expect:

* A step-by-step walkthrough of our Phone Dialer tools.
* Expert tips on effective communication with voters.
* Opportunities to ask questions and connect with other like-minded volunteers.


Sign up today and take the first step toward empowering voters and protecting democracy in 2025!

title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians
description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority,  and is published that it may go down to posterity.”  

The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.

But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting. No extant copies could be found.

The debate over the authenticity of the Mecklenburg Declaration began. And, when a copy of a document called the Mecklenburg Resolves written on May 30, 1775, was discovered in a 1775 newspaper, the debate intensified. The Resolves were revolutionary, but stopped short of declaring independence. Did both documents exist? Or was the Declaration being conflated with the Resolves?

Examine the evidence and decide for yourself by visiting the new exhibit, “Mecklenburg Declaration?” at the Presbyterian Heritage Center.

The PHC is open Tuesday-Friday (10-4) and Saturday (12-4).

title: Sold Out: Mexico’s Magical Migrations Institute
location: Toluca, Macho de Agua, and Puerto Vallarta, Mexico and Raleigh, N.C.
description:
Applications for the 2027 Mexico’s Magical Migrations Institute are now closed. 

Experience one of the world’s greatest migrations: monarch butterflies on their wintering grounds.Observe humpback whale social interactions.Visit and learn about the Mazahua people at La Casa de la Cultura Mazahua.Discover connections between Mexico and North Carolina.Participating educators will witness two of nature’s greatest spectacles – wintering monarch butterflies and humpback whales. Each year one of the world’s greatest migrations takes place as millions of monarch butterflies from the US and Canada travel south to the forested Mexican highlands. Once they arrive, they begin a period of winter hibernation by clustering together in huge numbers, blanketing the surrounding vegetation. As the butterflies are arriving in Mexico, so are humpback whales. Concluding their own incredible migration from their feeding waters off Alaska, large numbers of humpback whales gather off Mexico’s Pacific coast. They come to these warmer waters to breed and to give birth. Learn about these magical migrations from local experts and explore connections to North Carolina. We will share our adventures with students at home through daily blog posts from the field.

Dates: January 13-20, 2027. (Mandatory pre- and post-trip sessions will be held in Raleigh on Saturday, December 5, 2026 and Saturday, November 6, 2027.)

Locations: Toluca, Macho de Agua, and Puerto Vallarta, Mexico and Raleigh, N.C.

Group Size: Limited to 12 participants. (Note: We anticipate that Mexican teachers will join with American educators to form an international team.)

Activity Level: Moderate to rigorous including hiking (up to 2 miles) on uneven terrain, walking at high altitudes (~10,000 ft), and riding horses on trails with a guide.

Cost: $2200*
Includes round-trip airfare from Raleigh to Mexico, in-country transportation, instruction, lodging, and meals. Participants will be responsible for travel to and from Raleigh and expenses in Raleigh during pre- and post-trip sessions. See below for scholarship opportunities.

*The cost of all Institutes are significantly reduced thanks the generous support of the Friends of the Museum and the Goodnight Educational Foundation. Teachers that apply and are selected from the list of eastern counties (see below for details) may be eligible to receive a Simple Gifts Scholarship, which is provided through the generous support of the Simple Gifts Fund and the Anonymous Trust. 
 

Applications for Mexico’s Magical Migrations 2027 Institute are now closed. The application deadline was Monday, October 12, 2026.

Applications for Summer 2027 Institutes (Yellowstone and Blue Ridge) will open in November 2026.

title: Jan 21 - AI, ML and Computer Vision Meetup
description:
Raleigh AI, Machine Learning and Computer Vision Meetup
Join our virtual meetup to hear talks from experts on cutting-edge topics across AI, ML, and computer vision.

**Date, Time and Location**

Jan 21, 2027
9:00 AM - 11:00 AM PST
Online. **[Register for the Zoom!](https://voxel51.com/events/ai-ml-and-computer-vision-meetup-january-21-2027)**

**Verifier-Gated Generative Tutoring: When the LLM Writes Lessons but Never Decides Mastery**

Adaptive tutors increasingly let LLMs both generate content and decide mastery — a risky coupling. dino.study separates those roles: models draft interactive lessons under verifier gates, while deterministic Python BKT + FSRS tracks mastery and review timing. I'll show the production architecture (Expo app + Bun API + Postgres prerequisite graphs), cost (\~$0.04/lesson), and an honest LLM-simulated N=30/arm dry-run that is not a human peer-reviewed study.

The talk is code-forward with a live demo. Aimed at ML/CV practitioners curious about evaluation, mastery modeling, and shipping educational AI.

*About the Speaker*

[Animesh Alang](https://www.linkedin.com/in/animesh-alang-232713132) is a UCSC Computer Engineering junior building dino.study. He founded SlugAI, serves as President of CruzHacks, and was Cloud Track winner at NVIDIA Hack-a-Claw.

**Building CAD for Machine Intelligence: The Future of AI-Driven Engineering**

What does it take to build AI systems that can reason about geometry, design mechanical parts, and automate engineering workflows? In this talk, we introduce Quartz, a CAD system built for machine intelligence, and explore how high-performance geometry execution, reinforcement learning, and massively parallel environments enable AI agents to learn engineering through design and iteration.

We demonstrate how AI can create and modify complex assemblies while preserving editable CAD histories, and share our vision for the future of AI-driven engineering.

*About the Speaker*

[Debao Huang](https://www.linkedin.com/in/debao-huang/) is currently a Research Scientist at Spectral Labs, where he develops AI-native CAD systems and foundation models for automating engineering design. He obtained his Ph.D. in Electrical and Computer Engineering from The Ohio State University.

**Does 70% Mean 70%? Building an Honest Tennis Win-Probability Engine**

When a model says a tennis player has a 70% chance to win, does that player win 70% of the time? I built Tiebreak, a win-probability engine trained on about 900,000 ATP matches that layers surface-adjusted Elo, a point-by-point Markov chain and gradient boosting, updating live as a match unfolds.

Early versions looked better than they were because the same match leaked into both training and test data, and I show exactly how I caught it with a chronological, match-level split. Reliability diagrams then show where the model is calibrated and where it is overconfident.

Attendees leave with a practical checklist for building and honestly evaluating any ML model that outputs probabilities.

*About the Speaker*

[Krrish Ghindani](https://www.linkedin.com/in/krrishghindani/) is a Data Science junior at the University of San Francisco on a full merit scholarship and leads USF's Data Science team at national competitions (1st place).

**Can an Open-Weight Model Power a Physical AI Agent? Serving Gemma 4 on Google TPUs with Voxel51**

In this session, we'll deploy Google's Gemma 4 on Cloud TPUs using vLLM-TorchTPU and connect it to the Voxel51 Agent. Through a live demo and inference benchmarks, we'll explore how open-weight models can support Physical AI workflows, examining latency, throughput, and the infrastructure tradeoffs behind building reliable AI agents.

*About the Speaker*

[Adonai Vera](https://www.linkedin.com/in/adonai-vera/) is a Machine Learning Engineer and DevRel at Voxel51 with over 7 years of experience building computer vision and machine learning models using TensorFlow, Docker, and OpenCV.
source: Meetup: Raleigh AI, ML & Computer Vision

title: Applied Thematic Analysis
description:
It’s Monday morning and you open your qualitative research project folder. Thousands of pages of text, distributed across 90 in-depth interviews, await. What’s next? This workshop provides a roadmap for conducting an applied thematic analysis, through all major steps in the analytic process. Participants will learn the benefits of writing a qualitative data analysis plan, to ensure that the data collected are analyzed in a way that best informs the research question(s) and fulfills the study’s objectives.

The instructors will demonstrate how to inductively identify themes, transform those themes into codes, and aggregate codes into an evidence-based codebook that is easy to use and that will inform the study’s research question(s). Some time will be spent on the topic of integrating codes and interpreting thematic structure. Basic data reduction techniques will also be presented Hands-on exercises are included for those who wish to practice the concepts learned.

Registration and fee (refundable for UNCCH students upon attendance) are required for Zoom link access.

title: Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage
description: Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage at the Gregg Museum of Art & Design presents a series of vignettes exploring spaces of dignity, belonging, safety, and imagination within Black communities across North Carolina. Featuring historical photographs, contemporary images, artworks from the Gregg Museum collection including a handmade guitar by Freeman Vines, and ephemera from community partners, the exhibition reflects on place, memory, creativity, and spiritual resilience across generations. Through stories of triumph and adversity, Community Stories honors the ways Black Americans have sustained and uplifted their communities through family, entrepreneurship, cultural expression, and soulful imagination, while inspiring future generations.

title: Dr. Maria Ryan | UNC Music Research Forum
description:
Dr. Maria Ryan, Florida State University

“Title TBA”



 

Assistant Professor of Musicology Maria Ryan researches and writes about how African and African-descended people in the Americas theorized, performed, and listened to music with European origins in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. Ryan’s in-process book project, Ambivalent Listening: Race, Music, and Slavery in the British Colonial Caribbean 1750–1838, investigates the relationship between race and music in the British colonial Caribbean, exploring the many ways that African-descended musicians and listeners engaged with music with European origins. This work is supported in 2024–25 by an ACLS Fellowship, NEH Fellowship, and Citizens and Scholars Career Enhancement Fellowship. Early work from this project can be seen in the Journal of the Society for American Music and Journal of the American Musicological Society. In addition to her work on music in the British colonial Caribbean, Ryan researches and teaches Black feminist theory, the intellectual history of Black music, and book history and archive studies. Ryan is a Senior Fellow in Critical Bibliography at the Rare Book School, where she focuses on methods for recuperating Black listening practices from sources created under colonial logics. Ryan’s work has been supported by grants and fellowships from ACLS/Mellon, American Musicological Society, American Historical Association, Society for American Music, and Library Company of Philadelphia. She holds the B.A. degree from the University of Nottingham, the M.Mus. degree from King’s College London, and the Ph.D. in musicology with a certificate in Africana studies from the University of Pennsylvania.

 

The UNC Music Research Forum hosts invited lectures by distinguished music scholars from around the world and informal research presentations by members of our department and colleagues across campus. It serves as an intellectual hub for the department and is open to all. The Forum is usually held on the final Friday of each month during the semester from 3:30-5:00 pm in Person Recital Hall.

title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians
description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority,  and is published that it may go down to posterity.”  

The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.

But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting. No extant copies could be found.

The debate over the authenticity of the Mecklenburg Declaration began. And, when a copy of a document called the Mecklenburg Resolves written on May 30, 1775, was discovered in a 1775 newspaper, the debate intensified. The Resolves were revolutionary, but stopped short of declaring independence. Did both documents exist? Or was the Declaration being conflated with the Resolves?

Examine the evidence and decide for yourself by visiting the new exhibit, “Mecklenburg Declaration?” at the Presbyterian Heritage Center.

The PHC is open Tuesday-Friday (10-4) and Saturday (12-4).

title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians
description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority,  and is published that it may go down to posterity.”  

The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.

But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting. No extant copies could be found.

The debate over the authenticity of the Mecklenburg Declaration began. And, when a copy of a document called the Mecklenburg Resolves written on May 30, 1775, was discovered in a 1775 newspaper, the debate intensified. The Resolves were revolutionary, but stopped short of declaring independence. Did both documents exist? Or was the Declaration being conflated with the Resolves?

Examine the evidence and decide for yourself by visiting the new exhibit, “Mecklenburg Declaration?” at the Presbyterian Heritage Center.

The PHC is open Tuesday-Friday (10-4) and Saturday (12-4).

title: Introduction to Qualtrics
description:
Qualtrics is a powerful browser-based web-survey tool. It is available to UNC Chapel Hill faculty, staff, and students, for UNC-related projects. Qualtrics allows users to build complex surveys, distribute them, and analyze the responses all from one place.

 

In this course, we will cover basic Qualtrics functions beginning with an overview of survey options and settings, followed by hands-on practice programming and distributing a survey and downloading results. We will program some of the most common question and response types, customize requirements and validation, and add display logic, skip logic, and basic branch logic in the “survey flow”. We will then create and upload a contact list and discuss advantages and disadvantages of distributing the survey with a single reusable link vs. the survey mailer.  Finally, we will cover a basic overview of the Data & Analysis tab for viewing, editing, and exporting raw data into various formats including .csv, .tsv, .excel, and .spss. Other topics include project sharing/ collaboration, Groups and Libraries, and preventing fraudulent responses and bot activity.

 

This is an introductory course and will not cover the online analysis tools within Qualtrics. Please note, this is a hands-on, online course. All participants are required to create a Qualtrics account before the course. Carolina faculty, staff and students may create their free Qualtrics account here to access full features: http://qualtrics.unc.edu. Non-UNC affiliated participants can create a free trial account here: https://www.qualtrics.com/

 

Registration and fee (refundable for UNCCH students upon attendance) are required for Zoom link access. This event is sponsored by the UNC Odum Institute for Research in Social Science

title: NCMA Online Educator Course: Art and Math
description:
This self-paced, ten hour course explores points of integration between the K-8 North Carolina Essential Standards in Math and Visual Art. The course includes opportunities for educators to learn strategies for using art to identify math concepts, apply math skills to create art, and to reflect within a collaborative peer learning community. Participants will gain an understanding of best practices in arts integration and will become more familiar with the North Carolina Museum of Art’s collection.

Each course module is divided into three sections: Define, Explore, and Practice. In Define, we introduce concepts, vocabulary, and works of art to stimulate thinking and help you begin identifying points of integration between art and math. In Explore, we ask you to deeply engage in those points of integration through participating in visual thinking routines and short activities that uncover math within art. In Practice, you will engage in using math as the building blocks to create art by viewing teacher spotlight videos and exploring exemplar lesson ideas.  You will reflect on these various projects and select several that connect best with the mathematics standards that you teach, trying out those projects and planning how you would adapt them to your teaching.

The 7 Points of Integration covered in the course are:

ShapePatternSymmetryMeasurementCoordinate Points and PlanesRatio/FractionsData VisualizationThe course is aligned with the K–8 North Carolina Standard Course of Study for Visual Art and Math, which can be adapted to support foundational knowledge in secondary art and math courses. They are open to educators of all disciplines and audiences. A certificate of participation for 10 hours will be provided (1 CEU) with approval from the local school system. The course runs from January 27th - April 6th and educators can join at any point. Registration is now open. $18 Members, $20 Nonmembers.

title: Jan 27 - Physical AI, ML and Computer Vision Meetup: Purpose-Built Robots
description:
Raleigh AI, Machine Learning and Computer Vision Meetup
Join us for the Physical AI, ML and Computer Vision Meetup series focused on robotics use cases. In this session we will focus on purpose-built robots.

**Date, Time and Location**

Jan 27, 2027
9:00 AM - 11:00 AM PST
Online. **[Register for the Zoom!](https://voxel51.com/events/physical-ai-ml-and-computer-vision-meetup-purpose-built-robots-january-27-2027)**

**Building a Home Health Robot for Family Caregiving**

Home health is one of the most personal places a robot can work, and one of the least explored. Jacob will share how Rhem Labs is building a purpose-built tabletop robot and family app that help households keep track of health readings and daily routines, so changes in a loved one's health can be spotted earlier.

He will talk about what his own family's caregiving experience taught him about the problem, the design choices that come with building for older adults and caregivers, and how a robot earns trust in someone's home. Attendees will hear how a focused, single-purpose robot can make a real difference in everyday care.

*About the Speaker*

[Jacob Shen](https://www.linkedin.com/in/jacobshenn/) is founder and CEO of Rhem Labs, a Y Combinator company building Rhem, a tabletop robot for home health. After years of caring for relatives at home, he set out to build a robot and family app that track health readings and daily routines so families can spot changes earlier.

**Closing the Loop Between Sensing and Action in Surgical Robotics**

Some of the hardest robotics problems live inside the human body, where space is tight, visibility is limited and every millimeter counts. Ali will share how Mosaic Intelligence Labs is building purpose-built surgical robots that pair sensing catheters with robotic control to reduce reliance on X-ray guidance. She will explain why today's instruments lack a real feedback loop between what they sense and how they act, and how closing that loop opens the door to safer, more precise procedures. The talk will also cover what it takes to design a robot for a single, high-stakes job and the lessons that carry over to purpose-built robots in other fields.

*About the Speaker*

[Ali Mackanic](https://www.linkedin.com/in/a-kight/) is co-founder and Chief Technology Officer of Mosaic Intelligence Labs, a San Francisco company building sensing surgical robots. Her team is developing sensing catheters and robotic controls designed to reduce reliance on X-ray guidance during procedures, giving surgical instruments a real feedback loop between what they sense and how they act.

**Purpose-Built for People: The Invisible Metrics of Robot Adoption**

Your robot works. Accuracy is 0.1 mm, uptime is 24/7, the demo was flawless. Six months later, it sits switched off in a corner of the plant.

Robotics projects rarely fail on engineering metrics. They fail on the ones nobody measures: how much operators trust the robot, how a single bug is perceived, whether the robot solves the real bottleneck. Purpose-built robots have an edge here: designed around operators' real pain points, they start with trust instead of fighting for it.

Drawing on deployments in mining, oil and gas, manufacturing and pharma, Hugo Turlet walks through a real ROI breakdown, from OEE to adoption, and shows which hidden factors purpose-built design can move. Attendees will leave with a short list of invisible metrics, how to measure them, and how purpose-built design can move them.

*About the Speaker*

[Hugo Turlet](https://www.linkedin.com/in/hugo-turlet/) is a robotics engineer who leads the robotics practice at Osedea, a Montreal innovation firm. His strength is translation: he turns field needs into technical requirements, and those requirements into business models that work. A regular robotics and AI columnist on Montreal radio and an open-source contributor to Hugging Face, he works to make robotics accessible to everyone.

**Motivation and Challenges in working with Multimodal Timeseries Data**

Physical AI is having its moment, with many companies and research teams focussed on this space. But working with physical AI data means wrestling with high cardinality, complex, non-synced, multi sensor streams that are hard to explore, align and curate. In this talk, we will break down the challenges that come with multimodal time series data, and then look at the research directions this industry is pursuing, the ones that are unlocked when you can actually work with your data effectively.

*About the Speaker*

[Prerna Dhareshwar](https://www.linkedin.com/in/prernamd/) is a Machine Learning Engineer at Voxel51, where she helps customers leverage Voxel51 to accelerate dataset curation, model development, and evaluation in real-world AI workflows.

**Faster Physical AI Development with CoreWeave**

Building robots and autonomous systems means training on huge multimodal datasets, running simulation at scale, and iterating on models quickly. In this short session, CoreWeave's Head of Physical AI shares how teams are building their physical AI infrastructure today, where the bottlenecks are, and what is coming next to make it easier to go from data to deployed models.

*About the Speaker*

[Matt Shaffer](https://www.linkedin.com/in/shaffermatthew/) is a founder and research scientist, I have spent the last decade bridging the gap between frontier research and commercial reality. With a background spanning $44M+ in fundraising, product strategy, customer discovery, research, engineering, hiring, executive operations, and technical leadership, I have built and led distributed organizations to deliver AI-powered robotics across industries.
source: Meetup: Raleigh AI, ML & Computer Vision

title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians
description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority,  and is published that it may go down to posterity.”  

The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.

But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting. No extant copies could be found.

The debate over the authenticity of the Mecklenburg Declaration began. And, when a copy of a document called the Mecklenburg Resolves written on May 30, 1775, was discovered in a 1775 newspaper, the debate intensified. The Resolves were revolutionary, but stopped short of declaring independence. Did both documents exist? Or was the Declaration being conflated with the Resolves?

Examine the evidence and decide for yourself by visiting the new exhibit, “Mecklenburg Declaration?” at the Presbyterian Heritage Center.

The PHC is open Tuesday-Friday (10-4) and Saturday (12-4).

title: NCMA Online Educator Course: Art and Math
description:
This self-paced, ten hour course explores points of integration between the K-8 North Carolina Essential Standards in Math and Visual Art. The course includes opportunities for educators to learn strategies for using art to identify math concepts, apply math skills to create art, and to reflect within a collaborative peer learning community. Participants will gain an understanding of best practices in arts integration and will become more familiar with the North Carolina Museum of Art’s collection.

Each course module is divided into three sections: Define, Explore, and Practice. In Define, we introduce concepts, vocabulary, and works of art to stimulate thinking and help you begin identifying points of integration between art and math. In Explore, we ask you to deeply engage in those points of integration through participating in visual thinking routines and short activities that uncover math within art. In Practice, you will engage in using math as the building blocks to create art by viewing teacher spotlight videos and exploring exemplar lesson ideas.  You will reflect on these various projects and select several that connect best with the mathematics standards that you teach, trying out those projects and planning how you would adapt them to your teaching.

The 7 Points of Integration covered in the course are:

ShapePatternSymmetryMeasurementCoordinate Points and PlanesRatio/FractionsData VisualizationThe course is aligned with the K–8 North Carolina Standard Course of Study for Visual Art and Math, which can be adapted to support foundational knowledge in secondary art and math courses. They are open to educators of all disciplines and audiences. A certificate of participation for 10 hours will be provided (1 CEU) with approval from the local school system. The course runs from January 27th - April 6th and educators can join at any point. Registration is now open. $18 Members, $20 Nonmembers.

title: Introduction to Qualitative Interviewing
description:
While there are ranges of ways to conduct research, interviewing is the most common form of data collection in qualitative research, with over half of qualitative studies relying on interview-based data. Interviews are valuable because they afford researchers opportunities to learn how people understand, interpret, and make meaning of their experiences through direct engagement. This introductory course provides practical skills for both designing and conducting semi-structured qualitative interviews (along with a brief overview of structured and unstructured interviewing).

 

Using course participants’ research interests, we will develop interview protocols, practice conducting effective interviews—with emphasis on active listening and asking productive follow-up questions. Participants will learn to formulate open-ended questions, organize interview questions around a research question, and use interview probes to invite elaboration, clarification, and reflection. Through examples, discussion, and hands-on activities, we will consider how interviewing is a relational and interpretive process that also requires that researchers reflect on how their own perspectives shape assumptions and decision-making. This course is designed for beginning qualitative researchers and will offer practical opportunities and experiences to plan and conduct semi-structured interviews for qualitative research.

title: Temple Theatre Presents: "One Noble Journey"
description:

title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians
description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority,  and is published that it may go down to posterity.”  

The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.

But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting. No extant copies could be found.

The debate over the authenticity of the Mecklenburg Declaration began. And, when a copy of a document called the Mecklenburg Resolves written on May 30, 1775, was discovered in a 1775 newspaper, the debate intensified. The Resolves were revolutionary, but stopped short of declaring independence. Did both documents exist? Or was the Declaration being conflated with the Resolves?

Examine the evidence and decide for yourself by visiting the new exhibit, “Mecklenburg Declaration?” at the Presbyterian Heritage Center.

The PHC is open Tuesday-Friday (10-4) and Saturday (12-4).

title: NCMA Online Educator Course: Art and Math
description:
This self-paced, ten hour course explores points of integration between the K-8 North Carolina Essential Standards in Math and Visual Art. The course includes opportunities for educators to learn strategies for using art to identify math concepts, apply math skills to create art, and to reflect within a collaborative peer learning community. Participants will gain an understanding of best practices in arts integration and will become more familiar with the North Carolina Museum of Art’s collection.

Each course module is divided into three sections: Define, Explore, and Practice. In Define, we introduce concepts, vocabulary, and works of art to stimulate thinking and help you begin identifying points of integration between art and math. In Explore, we ask you to deeply engage in those points of integration through participating in visual thinking routines and short activities that uncover math within art. In Practice, you will engage in using math as the building blocks to create art by viewing teacher spotlight videos and exploring exemplar lesson ideas.  You will reflect on these various projects and select several that connect best with the mathematics standards that you teach, trying out those projects and planning how you would adapt them to your teaching.

The 7 Points of Integration covered in the course are:

ShapePatternSymmetryMeasurementCoordinate Points and PlanesRatio/FractionsData VisualizationThe course is aligned with the K–8 North Carolina Standard Course of Study for Visual Art and Math, which can be adapted to support foundational knowledge in secondary art and math courses. They are open to educators of all disciplines and audiences. A certificate of participation for 10 hours will be provided (1 CEU) with approval from the local school system. The course runs from January 27th - April 6th and educators can join at any point. Registration is now open. $18 Members, $20 Nonmembers.

title: Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage
description: Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage at the Gregg Museum of Art & Design presents a series of vignettes exploring spaces of dignity, belonging, safety, and imagination within Black communities across North Carolina. Featuring historical photographs, contemporary images, artworks from the Gregg Museum collection including a handmade guitar by Freeman Vines, and ephemera from community partners, the exhibition reflects on place, memory, creativity, and spiritual resilience across generations. Through stories of triumph and adversity, Community Stories honors the ways Black Americans have sustained and uplifted their communities through family, entrepreneurship, cultural expression, and soulful imagination, while inspiring future generations.

title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians
description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority,  and is published that it may go down to posterity.”  

The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.

But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting. No extant copies could be found.

The debate over the authenticity of the Mecklenburg Declaration began. And, when a copy of a document called the Mecklenburg Resolves written on May 30, 1775, was discovered in a 1775 newspaper, the debate intensified. The Resolves were revolutionary, but stopped short of declaring independence. Did both documents exist? Or was the Declaration being conflated with the Resolves?

Examine the evidence and decide for yourself by visiting the new exhibit, “Mecklenburg Declaration?” at the Presbyterian Heritage Center.

The PHC is open Tuesday-Friday (10-4) and Saturday (12-4).

title: NCMA Online Educator Course: Art and Math
description:
This self-paced, ten hour course explores points of integration between the K-8 North Carolina Essential Standards in Math and Visual Art. The course includes opportunities for educators to learn strategies for using art to identify math concepts, apply math skills to create art, and to reflect within a collaborative peer learning community. Participants will gain an understanding of best practices in arts integration and will become more familiar with the North Carolina Museum of Art’s collection.

Each course module is divided into three sections: Define, Explore, and Practice. In Define, we introduce concepts, vocabulary, and works of art to stimulate thinking and help you begin identifying points of integration between art and math. In Explore, we ask you to deeply engage in those points of integration through participating in visual thinking routines and short activities that uncover math within art. In Practice, you will engage in using math as the building blocks to create art by viewing teacher spotlight videos and exploring exemplar lesson ideas.  You will reflect on these various projects and select several that connect best with the mathematics standards that you teach, trying out those projects and planning how you would adapt them to your teaching.

The 7 Points of Integration covered in the course are:

ShapePatternSymmetryMeasurementCoordinate Points and PlanesRatio/FractionsData VisualizationThe course is aligned with the K–8 North Carolina Standard Course of Study for Visual Art and Math, which can be adapted to support foundational knowledge in secondary art and math courses. They are open to educators of all disciplines and audiences. A certificate of participation for 10 hours will be provided (1 CEU) with approval from the local school system. The course runs from January 27th - April 6th and educators can join at any point. Registration is now open. $18 Members, $20 Nonmembers.

title: Cognitive Interviewing in Survey Research
description:
Cognitive interviewing in survey research is a tool that allows researchers to improve survey questions and questionnaires by better understanding how respondents understand and respond to the questions they are being asked. Data gathered through cognitive interviews help researchers identify and remedy issues with their questionnaires. This short course provides participants with fundamentals on where cognitive interviews fit in the survey process and on how to design, conduct, and analyze cognitive interviews. Participants will have the opportunity to practice specific cognitive interviewing techniques, including think-alouds, probing, and observation. Participants will also learn about revising survey questions based on interpreting cognitive interview results and about the research on which cognitive interview practices are based.

Course Goals:
By the end of the course, participants will be able to:
1. Understand what cognitive interviews are and their use in survey research
2. Be able to prepare for and conduct cognitive interviews
3. Improve survey questionnaires and survey items based on cognitive interview data

 

Registration and fee (refundable for Carolina students) are required for Zoom link access.

This event is sponsored by the UNC Odum Institute.

title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians
description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority,  and is published that it may go down to posterity.”  

The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.

But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting. No extant copies could be found.

The debate over the authenticity of the Mecklenburg Declaration began. And, when a copy of a document called the Mecklenburg Resolves written on May 30, 1775, was discovered in a 1775 newspaper, the debate intensified. The Resolves were revolutionary, but stopped short of declaring independence. Did both documents exist? Or was the Declaration being conflated with the Resolves?

Examine the evidence and decide for yourself by visiting the new exhibit, “Mecklenburg Declaration?” at the Presbyterian Heritage Center.

The PHC is open Tuesday-Friday (10-4) and Saturday (12-4).

title: NCMA Online Educator Course: Art and Math
description:
This self-paced, ten hour course explores points of integration between the K-8 North Carolina Essential Standards in Math and Visual Art. The course includes opportunities for educators to learn strategies for using art to identify math concepts, apply math skills to create art, and to reflect within a collaborative peer learning community. Participants will gain an understanding of best practices in arts integration and will become more familiar with the North Carolina Museum of Art’s collection.

Each course module is divided into three sections: Define, Explore, and Practice. In Define, we introduce concepts, vocabulary, and works of art to stimulate thinking and help you begin identifying points of integration between art and math. In Explore, we ask you to deeply engage in those points of integration through participating in visual thinking routines and short activities that uncover math within art. In Practice, you will engage in using math as the building blocks to create art by viewing teacher spotlight videos and exploring exemplar lesson ideas.  You will reflect on these various projects and select several that connect best with the mathematics standards that you teach, trying out those projects and planning how you would adapt them to your teaching.

The 7 Points of Integration covered in the course are:

ShapePatternSymmetryMeasurementCoordinate Points and PlanesRatio/FractionsData VisualizationThe course is aligned with the K–8 North Carolina Standard Course of Study for Visual Art and Math, which can be adapted to support foundational knowledge in secondary art and math courses. They are open to educators of all disciplines and audiences. A certificate of participation for 10 hours will be provided (1 CEU) with approval from the local school system. The course runs from January 27th - April 6th and educators can join at any point. Registration is now open. $18 Members, $20 Nonmembers.

title: Project RESTORE Educator Trek: Where Swans Fly, Bears Walk, and Wolves Howl
location: North Carolina Museum of Natural Sciences
description:
Experience one of the greatest wildlife spectacles in North Carolina – thousands of tundra swans, snow geese, and other waterfowl over-wintering in an area rich in wildlife such as black bears, bobcats and red wolves. Learn winter bird identification, tips on preserving tracks and signs, and ideas for incorporating wild creatures into your teaching. We hope to have the opportunity to meet with a red wolf biologist to learn about the restoration and monitoring work being done with this endangered species.

With support from the US Fish and Wildlife Service, Project RESTORE (Rescuing Endangered Species Through Outreach, Restoration, and Education) will feature a suite of educational opportunities for teachers and students to participate in restoration and monitoring of imperiled and endangered species in eastern North Carolina.

Credit: 20 contact hours toward CEUs or Criteria II/III for North Carolina’s Environmental Education Certification Program

Lodging: The workshop fee covers a two-night hotel stay near the wildlife refuge, double occupancy.

Transportation: Participants can ride with the group from Raleigh departing at 2pm or meet us in Columbia, NC in the evening. Transportation will be in Museum vans.

Registration: register now! 

If the workshop is full when you go to register, please sign up for the waiting list!

*The cost of this Trek is reduced due to a grant through the US Fish and Wildlife Service. Due to this reduction of costs, Friends of the Museum discounts are unavailable.

Details:

Fee: $170* (includes two nights double-occupancy hotel style lodging, transportation, and workshop materials)Requirements: For educators (includes teachers, administrators, pre-service or substitute teachers; non-formal educators; any adult working on their EE certification)Program Instructor(s): Megan Davis, Danielle Pender, Rory McCollum and local expertsActivity Level: Hiking 2-3 miles on uneven surfaces.
