title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians
description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority,  and is published that it may go down to posterity.”  

The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.

But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting. No extant copies could be found.

The debate over the authenticity of the Mecklenburg Declaration began. And, when a copy of a document called the Mecklenburg Resolves written on May 30, 1775, was discovered in a 1775 newspaper, the debate intensified. The Resolves were revolutionary, but stopped short of declaring independence. Did both documents exist? Or was the Declaration being conflated with the Resolves?

Examine the evidence and decide for yourself by visiting the new exhibit, “Mecklenburg Declaration?” at the Presbyterian Heritage Center.

The PHC is open Tuesday-Friday (10-4) and Saturday (12-4).

title: NCMA Online Educator Course: Art and Math
description:
This self-paced, ten hour course explores points of integration between the K-8 North Carolina Essential Standards in Math and Visual Art. The course includes opportunities for educators to learn strategies for using art to identify math concepts, apply math skills to create art, and to reflect within a collaborative peer learning community. Participants will gain an understanding of best practices in arts integration and will become more familiar with the North Carolina Museum of Art’s collection.

Each course module is divided into three sections: Define, Explore, and Practice. In Define, we introduce concepts, vocabulary, and works of art to stimulate thinking and help you begin identifying points of integration between art and math. In Explore, we ask you to deeply engage in those points of integration through participating in visual thinking routines and short activities that uncover math within art. In Practice, you will engage in using math as the building blocks to create art by viewing teacher spotlight videos and exploring exemplar lesson ideas.  You will reflect on these various projects and select several that connect best with the mathematics standards that you teach, trying out those projects and planning how you would adapt them to your teaching.

The 7 Points of Integration covered in the course are:

ShapePatternSymmetryMeasurementCoordinate Points and PlanesRatio/FractionsData VisualizationThe course is aligned with the K–8 North Carolina Standard Course of Study for Visual Art and Math, which can be adapted to support foundational knowledge in secondary art and math courses. They are open to educators of all disciplines and audiences. A certificate of participation for 10 hours will be provided (1 CEU) with approval from the local school system. The course runs from January 27th - April 6th and educators can join at any point. Registration is now open. $18 Members, $20 Nonmembers.

title: Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage
description: Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage at the Gregg Museum of Art & Design presents a series of vignettes exploring spaces of dignity, belonging, safety, and imagination within Black communities across North Carolina. Featuring historical photographs, contemporary images, artworks from the Gregg Museum collection including a handmade guitar by Freeman Vines, and ephemera from community partners, the exhibition reflects on place, memory, creativity, and spiritual resilience across generations. Through stories of triumph and adversity, Community Stories honors the ways Black Americans have sustained and uplifted their communities through family, entrepreneurship, cultural expression, and soulful imagination, while inspiring future generations.

title: Interprofessional Design-a-thon
description:
The Interprofessional Design-a-thon brings together student teams to apply human-centered design thinking to address patient needs. Student teams collaborate on a solution and present their idea to a panel of faculty and health professionals, who then select a winning team. This is an approved IPEP Distinguished Scholars Immersion hosted by the Office of Interprofessional Education and Practice.

 

Fall 2026 Design-a-thon:

Saturday, January 30 from 10 a.m. to 3 p.m.

Saturday, February 6 from 10 a.m. to 3 p.m.

 

Design-a-thon Eligibility:

Complete basic BEAM Makerspace training.Be available all 5 hours on each Saturday (10 hours total) and complete independent work (research, faculty consultation, etc.) in the week between.Designed for medical, nursing, biomedical engineering, physical therapy, clinical rehabilitation and mental health counseling, occupational therapy, speech therapy and pharmacy students. Other students can apply, and their participation will be considered as space allows.​Applications are reviewed as received and the priority deadline to apply is December 1, 2026. Questions? Email unc_ipe@unc.edu.

title: Project RESTORE Educator Trek: Where Swans Fly, Bears Walk, and Wolves Howl
location: North Carolina Museum of Natural Sciences
description:
Experience one of the greatest wildlife spectacles in North Carolina – thousands of tundra swans, snow geese, and other waterfowl over-wintering in an area rich in wildlife such as black bears, bobcats and red wolves. Learn winter bird identification, tips on preserving tracks and signs, and ideas for incorporating wild creatures into your teaching. We hope to have the opportunity to meet with a red wolf biologist to learn about the restoration and monitoring work being done with this endangered species.

With support from the US Fish and Wildlife Service, Project RESTORE (Rescuing Endangered Species Through Outreach, Restoration, and Education) will feature a suite of educational opportunities for teachers and students to participate in restoration and monitoring of imperiled and endangered species in eastern North Carolina.

Credit: 20 contact hours toward CEUs or Criteria II/III for North Carolina’s Environmental Education Certification Program

Lodging: The workshop fee covers a two-night hotel stay near the wildlife refuge, double occupancy.

Transportation: Participants can ride with the group from Raleigh departing at 2pm or meet us in Columbia, NC in the evening. Transportation will be in Museum vans.

Registration: register now! 

If the workshop is full when you go to register, please sign up for the waiting list!

*The cost of this Trek is reduced due to a grant through the US Fish and Wildlife Service. Due to this reduction of costs, Friends of the Museum discounts are unavailable.

Details:

Fee: $170* (includes two nights double-occupancy hotel style lodging, transportation, and workshop materials)Requirements: For educators (includes teachers, administrators, pre-service or substitute teachers; non-formal educators; any adult working on their EE certification)Program Instructor(s): Megan Davis, Danielle Pender, Rory McCollum and local expertsActivity Level: Hiking 2-3 miles on uneven surfaces.

title: Durham Social Hack Night
description:
Triangle Developers
Hey tech folks, come out and hang at Hi-Wire starting at 6pm! Hack Night is meant to be a social evening for folks in tech. It's less about networking and more about community.

**Look for the Hack Night tabletop sign** and nerds wearing name tags to find us. If the weather is nice, we'll probably be outside.

Help folks feel welcome by using the **"Pac Man Rule"** \- when standing with a group of people \(usually in a circle\)\, leave some space open so that another person can easily join\.

See our [Code of Conduct](https://github.com/TriangleDevsSlack/policies/blob/master/code-of-conduct.md). To summarize: be nice or leave. No tolerance for harassment or oppression. In addition, since alcohol is present at these events, please be mindful of your consumption and respect other people's choices on whether or not to consume.

**FAQs**
*Do folks hack at Hack Night? Should I bring my computer?*
This is more of a night for hackers than an actual hack night. You're welcome to bring a laptop, but most people will only be socializing.

*What are the beverage options? Are there any non-alcoholic drinks?*
Hi-Wire Brewing offers many types of beers including a few non-alcoholic options plus wine and some liquor. They usually have a happy hour special on the first few beers on the menu. In the same complex are Cugino Forno which has additional drink options, and Two Roosters which has excellent ice cream.

*Are there any drink specials?*
If Hack Night is on a Tuesday, Hi-Wire usually has $5 pints for their flagship beers. Look for the list at the counter.

*Do people eat snacks/dinner during the meetup?*
Sometimes folks will order a pizza or salad from Cugino Forno. I sometimes grab an ice cream from Two Roosters across the way. Most people eat before or after but it's no big deal - whatever you prefer and are most comfortable with.

*How can I connect with the developer community?*
Go to [triangledevelopers.com](https://triangledevelopers.com/) to find the Discord and Slack info.

title: Designing AI-Assisted Qualitative Research Workflows
description:
This workshop will introduce participants to a framework for considering the consequences of using generative AI in qualitative research designs and workflows (Paulus, 2023; Paulus & Lester, 2024). We will start by defining digital research workflows and how to engage in technological reflexivity throughout the design process. We will learn how to distinguish between methodological strategies and technological tactics, i.e. why researchers must first know what they want to do before choosing the best tools for doing it (Woolf & Silver, 2018). We will then discuss the genres of AI-assist technologies currently available to qualitative researchers and how to select the most appropriate platform.

 

MAXQDA AI-Assist tools will be used to illustrate tactics currently available to researchers. Next we will consider the consequences of AI-Assisted workflows, acknowledging dilemmas such as how generative AI is challenging the essence of what it means to do qualitative work (Paulus & Marone, 2025; Paulus, Lester & Davis, 2026). Finally, we will discuss best practices for how to transparently report and evaluate researcher use of AI (Lester & Paulus, 2026). Workshop time will alternate between short lectures and demonstrations and small-group discussion and application activities.

 

Registration and fee (refundable for UNCCH students) are required. This event is sponsored by the UNC Odum Institute for Research.

title: Feb 10 - Physical AI Meetup: Robot Brains and Models
description:
Raleigh AI, Machine Learning and Computer Vision Meetup
Join us for the Physical AI, ML and Computer Vision Meetup series focused on robotics use cases. In this session we will focus on robot brains and models.

**Date, Time and Location**

Feb 10, 2027
9:00 AM - 11:00 AM PST
Online. **[Register for the Zoom!](https://voxel51.com/events/physical-ai-ml-and-computer-vision-meetup-robot-brains-and-models-february-10-2027)**

**Physical AI That Adapts**

Every vision model is trained on a snapshot of the world, but robots are deployed into one that keeps changing: lighting shifts, friction drifts, objects move, actuators wear. Today the fix is a slow loop of collecting new data, retraining, validating and redeploying, which can take weeks or months. In this talk, we show how Lazy Dynamics’ LazyInfer closes that gap by treating perception, parameter learning and control as one Bayesian inference problem that runs on the device, inside the control loop.

*About the Speaker*

[Bart van Erp](https://www.linkedin.com/in/bart-van-erp/) is CTO at Lazy Dynamics. He has a background in Electrical Engineering and a PhD in the field of probabilistic machine learning.

**Robotic World Models: Cloud Versus On-Edge**

Cloud-hosted robotic world models can draw on substantial compute, while on-edge models promise local, low-latency inference; choosing between them depends on the reliability of their predictions. We examine this question through a from-scratch, gradient-verified reproduction of the proprioceptive Robotic World Model for ANYmal D, using recorded robot trajectories and CPU resources. Autoregressive training reproduces the model's long-horizon advantage over teacher forcing, while ensemble disagreement tracks the ordering of prediction errors but substantially underestimates their magnitude. On the released checkpoint's training episodes, disagreement is 33.4 times smaller than realized error at the method's 100-step rollout horizon, making it a useful ranking signal but not a calibrated error bar.

*About the Speaker*

Joyjeet Singh is an independent researcher in physics-informed machine learning and the sole author of three arXiv preprints on implicit-reasoning models, world-model reproducibility, and the planning objectives used over learned latent dynamics.

**Faster Physical AI Development with CoreWeave**

Robot brains are getting bigger. Vision language action models, world models and foundation policies all demand large training runs, fast experimentation and serving that keeps up with real robots. In this session, Narendra Kumar Vadapalli, Senior Specialist Field Engineer at CoreWeave, walks through how physical AI teams are building the infrastructure behind these models today. Drawing on his work helping customers design and scale AI platforms on Kubernetes, he will cover how teams organize multimodal training data, run distributed training and simulation side by side, and move models from experiment to deployment without rebuilding their stack each time. Attendees will leave with practical patterns for scaling robot learning workloads and a look at what is coming next.

title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians
description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority,  and is published that it may go down to posterity.”  

The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.

But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting. No extant copies could be found.

The debate over the authenticity of the Mecklenburg Declaration began. And, when a copy of a document called the Mecklenburg Resolves written on May 30, 1775, was discovered in a 1775 newspaper, the debate intensified. The Resolves were revolutionary, but stopped short of declaring independence. Did both documents exist? Or was the Declaration being conflated with the Resolves?

Examine the evidence and decide for yourself by visiting the new exhibit, “Mecklenburg Declaration?” at the Presbyterian Heritage Center.

The PHC is open Tuesday-Friday (10-4) and Saturday (12-4).

title: NCMA Online Educator Course: Art and Math
description:
This self-paced, ten hour course explores points of integration between the K-8 North Carolina Essential Standards in Math and Visual Art. The course includes opportunities for educators to learn strategies for using art to identify math concepts, apply math skills to create art, and to reflect within a collaborative peer learning community. Participants will gain an understanding of best practices in arts integration and will become more familiar with the North Carolina Museum of Art’s collection.

Each course module is divided into three sections: Define, Explore, and Practice. In Define, we introduce concepts, vocabulary, and works of art to stimulate thinking and help you begin identifying points of integration between art and math. In Explore, we ask you to deeply engage in those points of integration through participating in visual thinking routines and short activities that uncover math within art. In Practice, you will engage in using math as the building blocks to create art by viewing teacher spotlight videos and exploring exemplar lesson ideas.  You will reflect on these various projects and select several that connect best with the mathematics standards that you teach, trying out those projects and planning how you would adapt them to your teaching.

The 7 Points of Integration covered in the course are:

ShapePatternSymmetryMeasurementCoordinate Points and PlanesRatio/FractionsData VisualizationThe course is aligned with the K–8 North Carolina Standard Course of Study for Visual Art and Math, which can be adapted to support foundational knowledge in secondary art and math courses. They are open to educators of all disciplines and audiences. A certificate of participation for 10 hours will be provided (1 CEU) with approval from the local school system. The course runs from January 27th - April 6th and educators can join at any point. Registration is now open. $18 Members, $20 Nonmembers.

title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians
description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority,  and is published that it may go down to posterity.”  

The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.

But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting. No extant copies could be found.

The debate over the authenticity of the Mecklenburg Declaration began. And, when a copy of a document called the Mecklenburg Resolves written on May 30, 1775, was discovered in a 1775 newspaper, the debate intensified. The Resolves were revolutionary, but stopped short of declaring independence. Did both documents exist? Or was the Declaration being conflated with the Resolves?

Examine the evidence and decide for yourself by visiting the new exhibit, “Mecklenburg Declaration?” at the Presbyterian Heritage Center.

The PHC is open Tuesday-Friday (10-4) and Saturday (12-4).

title: NCMA Online Educator Course: Art and Math
description:
This self-paced, ten hour course explores points of integration between the K-8 North Carolina Essential Standards in Math and Visual Art. The course includes opportunities for educators to learn strategies for using art to identify math concepts, apply math skills to create art, and to reflect within a collaborative peer learning community. Participants will gain an understanding of best practices in arts integration and will become more familiar with the North Carolina Museum of Art’s collection.

Each course module is divided into three sections: Define, Explore, and Practice. In Define, we introduce concepts, vocabulary, and works of art to stimulate thinking and help you begin identifying points of integration between art and math. In Explore, we ask you to deeply engage in those points of integration through participating in visual thinking routines and short activities that uncover math within art. In Practice, you will engage in using math as the building blocks to create art by viewing teacher spotlight videos and exploring exemplar lesson ideas.  You will reflect on these various projects and select several that connect best with the mathematics standards that you teach, trying out those projects and planning how you would adapt them to your teaching.

The 7 Points of Integration covered in the course are:

ShapePatternSymmetryMeasurementCoordinate Points and PlanesRatio/FractionsData VisualizationThe course is aligned with the K–8 North Carolina Standard Course of Study for Visual Art and Math, which can be adapted to support foundational knowledge in secondary art and math courses. They are open to educators of all disciplines and audiences. A certificate of participation for 10 hours will be provided (1 CEU) with approval from the local school system. The course runs from January 27th - April 6th and educators can join at any point. Registration is now open. $18 Members, $20 Nonmembers.

title: Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage
description: Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage at the Gregg Museum of Art & Design presents a series of vignettes exploring spaces of dignity, belonging, safety, and imagination within Black communities across North Carolina. Featuring historical photographs, contemporary images, artworks from the Gregg Museum collection including a handmade guitar by Freeman Vines, and ephemera from community partners, the exhibition reflects on place, memory, creativity, and spiritual resilience across generations. Through stories of triumph and adversity, Community Stories honors the ways Black Americans have sustained and uplifted their communities through family, entrepreneurship, cultural expression, and soulful imagination, while inspiring future generations.

title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians
description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority,  and is published that it may go down to posterity.”  

The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.

But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting. No extant copies could be found.

The debate over the authenticity of the Mecklenburg Declaration began. And, when a copy of a document called the Mecklenburg Resolves written on May 30, 1775, was discovered in a 1775 newspaper, the debate intensified. The Resolves were revolutionary, but stopped short of declaring independence. Did both documents exist? Or was the Declaration being conflated with the Resolves?

Examine the evidence and decide for yourself by visiting the new exhibit, “Mecklenburg Declaration?” at the Presbyterian Heritage Center.

The PHC is open Tuesday-Friday (10-4) and Saturday (12-4).

title: NCMA Online Educator Course: Art and Math
description:
This self-paced, ten hour course explores points of integration between the K-8 North Carolina Essential Standards in Math and Visual Art. The course includes opportunities for educators to learn strategies for using art to identify math concepts, apply math skills to create art, and to reflect within a collaborative peer learning community. Participants will gain an understanding of best practices in arts integration and will become more familiar with the North Carolina Museum of Art’s collection.

Each course module is divided into three sections: Define, Explore, and Practice. In Define, we introduce concepts, vocabulary, and works of art to stimulate thinking and help you begin identifying points of integration between art and math. In Explore, we ask you to deeply engage in those points of integration through participating in visual thinking routines and short activities that uncover math within art. In Practice, you will engage in using math as the building blocks to create art by viewing teacher spotlight videos and exploring exemplar lesson ideas.  You will reflect on these various projects and select several that connect best with the mathematics standards that you teach, trying out those projects and planning how you would adapt them to your teaching.

The 7 Points of Integration covered in the course are:

ShapePatternSymmetryMeasurementCoordinate Points and PlanesRatio/FractionsData VisualizationThe course is aligned with the K–8 North Carolina Standard Course of Study for Visual Art and Math, which can be adapted to support foundational knowledge in secondary art and math courses. They are open to educators of all disciplines and audiences. A certificate of participation for 10 hours will be provided (1 CEU) with approval from the local school system. The course runs from January 27th - April 6th and educators can join at any point. Registration is now open. $18 Members, $20 Nonmembers.

title: Designing Web Surveys
description:
This course will introduce methods for effectively designing web surveys to mitigate common mistakes that impact data quality and introduce measurement error. The course will focus on the following elements of web survey design – overall formatting and visual layout of screens, selecting and designing questions and response options (e.g., radio buttons, check boxes, grids, and open text fields), error and validation messaging, navigation elements, and usability. Special considerations for designing web surveys to accommodate mobile response will also be covered. This course will also offer practical guidance on selecting appropriate web survey platforms. However, this course will not provide instruction on the technical aspects of web survey programming or introduce programming languages. The course will draw from empirical literature on best practices coupled with practical considerations when designing and implementing web surveys.

Registration and fee (refundable for UNCCH students upon attendance) are required for Zoom link access.

title: Social Media as Qualitative Data: A Design Framework
description:
Conversations that take place online – from learning management systems to Signal chats to Discord groups to Reddit support groups and Instagram influencing – can be valuable forms of evidence for qualitative researchers. In this workshop, participants will create their own research designs to investigate a phenomenon of interest, as evidenced through social media data, in a systematic and rigorous way. The Paulus and Wise research design decision framework will scaffold learners in how to identify an object of interest; articulate their philosophical and theoretical assumptions about how language functions online; create focused and relevant research questions; ensure methodological alignment across aspects of the study design; resolve ethical dilemmas around treating social media as data; extract and transform social media into a coherent dataset; select appropriate technologies for managing and analyzing data; perform a systematic narrative, discourse and/or thematic analysis; and establish the quality of the findings. Course material will be drawn from “Looking for Learning, Insight and Transformation in Online Talk” (Paulus & Wise, Routledge, 2019).

Registration and fee are required for Zoom link access. Space is limited! Please visit course website for more information and registration.

title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians
description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority,  and is published that it may go down to posterity.”  

The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.

But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting. No extant copies could be found.

The debate over the authenticity of the Mecklenburg Declaration began. And, when a copy of a document called the Mecklenburg Resolves written on May 30, 1775, was discovered in a 1775 newspaper, the debate intensified. The Resolves were revolutionary, but stopped short of declaring independence. Did both documents exist? Or was the Declaration being conflated with the Resolves?

Examine the evidence and decide for yourself by visiting the new exhibit, “Mecklenburg Declaration?” at the Presbyterian Heritage Center.

The PHC is open Tuesday-Friday (10-4) and Saturday (12-4).

title: NCMA Online Educator Course: Art and Math
description:
This self-paced, ten hour course explores points of integration between the K-8 North Carolina Essential Standards in Math and Visual Art. The course includes opportunities for educators to learn strategies for using art to identify math concepts, apply math skills to create art, and to reflect within a collaborative peer learning community. Participants will gain an understanding of best practices in arts integration and will become more familiar with the North Carolina Museum of Art’s collection.

Each course module is divided into three sections: Define, Explore, and Practice. In Define, we introduce concepts, vocabulary, and works of art to stimulate thinking and help you begin identifying points of integration between art and math. In Explore, we ask you to deeply engage in those points of integration through participating in visual thinking routines and short activities that uncover math within art. In Practice, you will engage in using math as the building blocks to create art by viewing teacher spotlight videos and exploring exemplar lesson ideas.  You will reflect on these various projects and select several that connect best with the mathematics standards that you teach, trying out those projects and planning how you would adapt them to your teaching.

The 7 Points of Integration covered in the course are:

ShapePatternSymmetryMeasurementCoordinate Points and PlanesRatio/FractionsData VisualizationThe course is aligned with the K–8 North Carolina Standard Course of Study for Visual Art and Math, which can be adapted to support foundational knowledge in secondary art and math courses. They are open to educators of all disciplines and audiences. A certificate of participation for 10 hours will be provided (1 CEU) with approval from the local school system. The course runs from January 27th - April 6th and educators can join at any point. Registration is now open. $18 Members, $20 Nonmembers.

title: NCMA Online Educator Course: Art and Math
description:
This self-paced, ten hour course explores points of integration between the K-8 North Carolina Essential Standards in Math and Visual Art. The course includes opportunities for educators to learn strategies for using art to identify math concepts, apply math skills to create art, and to reflect within a collaborative peer learning community. Participants will gain an understanding of best practices in arts integration and will become more familiar with the North Carolina Museum of Art’s collection.

Each course module is divided into three sections: Define, Explore, and Practice. In Define, we introduce concepts, vocabulary, and works of art to stimulate thinking and help you begin identifying points of integration between art and math. In Explore, we ask you to deeply engage in those points of integration through participating in visual thinking routines and short activities that uncover math within art. In Practice, you will engage in using math as the building blocks to create art by viewing teacher spotlight videos and exploring exemplar lesson ideas.  You will reflect on these various projects and select several that connect best with the mathematics standards that you teach, trying out those projects and planning how you would adapt them to your teaching.

The 7 Points of Integration covered in the course are:

ShapePatternSymmetryMeasurementCoordinate Points and PlanesRatio/FractionsData VisualizationThe course is aligned with the K–8 North Carolina Standard Course of Study for Visual Art and Math, which can be adapted to support foundational knowledge in secondary art and math courses. They are open to educators of all disciplines and audiences. A certificate of participation for 10 hours will be provided (1 CEU) with approval from the local school system. The course runs from January 27th - April 6th and educators can join at any point. Registration is now open. $18 Members, $20 Nonmembers.

title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians
description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority,  and is published that it may go down to posterity.”  

The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.

But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting. No extant copies could be found.

The debate over the authenticity of the Mecklenburg Declaration began. And, when a copy of a document called the Mecklenburg Resolves written on May 30, 1775, was discovered in a 1775 newspaper, the debate intensified. The Resolves were revolutionary, but stopped short of declaring independence. Did both documents exist? Or was the Declaration being conflated with the Resolves?

Examine the evidence and decide for yourself by visiting the new exhibit, “Mecklenburg Declaration?” at the Presbyterian Heritage Center.

The PHC is open Tuesday-Friday (10-4) and Saturday (12-4).

title: AI Agents in Survey Research: Foundations, Applications, Oversight, and Evaluation
description:
This course explores the emerging role of AI agents in survey research. Designed for survey practitioners, data scientists, and social scientists, it introduces agentic AI as the next iteration of artificial intelligence technologies to be integrated with survey research methods. Building on foundational concepts in generative AI, the course examines how agents differ from the previous iteration of LLMs and considers their potential uses across the survey research lifecycle.
Participants will learn core technical concepts around agentic AI, approaches to evaluating agent performance in the survey context, the challenges of designing, implementing, and assessing agentic workflows, responsible AI deployment, AI-assisted vs AI-driven paradigms of work, and the role of human expertise in survey research. We will also examine bias in agentic systems, the implications of delegating research tasks to AI, and strategies for maintaining meaningful human oversight. Using data harmonization as a central application, the course will draw on emerging empirical research and practical examples to explore both the opportunities and limitations of agentic AI in survey research.

Registration and fee (refundable for UNCCH students upon attendance) are required for Zoom link access.

title: Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage
description: Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage at the Gregg Museum of Art & Design presents a series of vignettes exploring spaces of dignity, belonging, safety, and imagination within Black communities across North Carolina. Featuring historical photographs, contemporary images, artworks from the Gregg Museum collection including a handmade guitar by Freeman Vines, and ephemera from community partners, the exhibition reflects on place, memory, creativity, and spiritual resilience across generations. Through stories of triumph and adversity, Community Stories honors the ways Black Americans have sustained and uplifted their communities through family, entrepreneurship, cultural expression, and soulful imagination, while inspiring future generations.

title: 2027 Frank B. Hanes Writer-in-Residence Reading with Maggie Smith
description:
Maggie Smith, 2027 Frank B. Hanes Writer-in-Residence will give a reading on Tuesday, Feb 23, 2027 at 7:30pm. The Reading is free and open to the public.

 

Maggie Smith is the New York Times bestselling author of You Could Make This Place Beautiful; The People’s Project, an anthology co-curated with Saeed Jones; My Thoughts Have Wings, a picture book illustrated by SCBWI Portfolio grand prize winner Leanne Hatch; the national bestsellers Dear Writer: Pep Talks & Practical Advice for the Creative Life, Goldenrod, and Keep Moving: Notes on Loss, Creativity, and Change; as well as Good Bones, named one of the Best Five Poetry Books of 2017 by the Washington Post and winner of the 2018 Independent Publisher Book Awards Gold Medal in Poetry; The Well Speaks of Its Own Poison, winner of the 2012 Dorset Prize and the 2016 Independent Publisher Book Awards Gold Medal in Poetry; and Lamp of the Body, winner of the 2003 Benjamin Saltman Award. Smith’s 2026 book, A Suit or a Suitcase, is a collection of poems (Washington Square Press/Atria).

 

A 2011 recipient of a Creative Writing Fellowship from the National Endowment for the Arts, Smith has also received six Individual Excellence Awards from the Ohio Arts Council, two Academy of American Poets Prizes, a Pushcart Prize, and fellowships from the Sustainable Arts Foundation and the Virginia Center for the Creative Arts. Her poems have been widely published and anthologized, appearing in Best American Poetry, the New York Times, The New Yorker, Tin House, The Believer, The Paris Review, Poetry, Ploughshares, the Kenyon Review, The Gettysburg Review, The Iowa Review, The Southern Review, and Virginia Quarterly Review. Her essays have been published in the New York Times, the Washington Post, on the Poetry Foundation website, and elsewhere.

 

In 2016 Maggie Smith’s poem “Good Bones” went viral internationally, receiving coverage in the Washington Post, the Guardian, the Telegraph, Slate, Huffington Post Italia, and elsewhere. To date it has been translated into nearly a dozen languages; interpreted by a dance troupe in Chennai, India; and set to music by multiple composers. PRI (Public Radio International) called it “the official poem of 2016.” In 2017 the poem was featured on an episode of the CBS primetime drama Madam Secretary, also called “Good Bones,” and was read by Meryl Streep at Lincoln Center.

title: AI for Research (AIR) – Introduction to AI Tools in Qualitative Software
description:
Discover how artificial intelligence can streamline workflows, uncover hidden patterns, and empower breakthroughs in your field. Learn practical applications of AI through Odum Institute AIR series that can revolutionize your research process.

This course will introduce participants to generative AI tools in qualitative software—ATLAS.ti, MAXQDA, and NVivo. These tools can be used to summarize textual documents through AI-assisted memo writing and to support coding, with each program taking a different approach to integrating human judgment and AI features.

The course will also demonstrate how ChatGPT can be used to code textual data, how to create effective prompts, and how to import results from ChatGPT into qualitative software for further analysis. The course will be based on presentation and lecture but will provide brief exercises for hands-on exercises to be completed outside of the course.

Registration and fee (refundable upon attendance of course) are required for Zoom link access. Must have an active UNCCH Onyen to register.

title: Conducting Qualitative Thematic Analysis Without Coding
description:
Thematic analysis is a widely used and useful approach for analyzing qualitative data, but developing themes does not have to involve coding. This workshop introduces alternative, creative approaches to thematic analysis that invite researchers to engage deeply with qualitative data through practices such as annotation, close reading, and poetic analysis. Participants will explore how to identify patterns of meaning, to attend to language and expression in data, and to develop interpretive insights without relying on a formal coding process. Through examples, discussion, and hands-on activities, participants will experiment with ways of engaging with their data, including noticing resonances and tensions across data and using poetic techniques to explore and emphasize the meanings, emotions, and experiences expressed in qualitative materials.

 

The workshop also considers how researchers make interpretive decisions, move from close engagement with individual accounts to broader patterns of meaning, and develop themes that remain grounded in the data. Emphasizing curiosity, reflexivity, and interpretive creativity, this workshop offers different pathways for researchers who want to expand their analytic practices beyond coding and to explore new ways of making meaning with qualitative data. Participants are encouraged to bring and use some of your own qualitative data, or if you do not have data yet, some will be supplied.

 

Registration and fee (refundable for UNCCH students) are required. This event is sponsored by the UNC Odum Institue for Research.

title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians
description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority,  and is published that it may go down to posterity.”  

The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.

But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting. No extant copies could be found.

The debate over the authenticity of the Mecklenburg Declaration began. And, when a copy of a document called the Mecklenburg Resolves written on May 30, 1775, was discovered in a 1775 newspaper, the debate intensified. The Resolves were revolutionary, but stopped short of declaring independence. Did both documents exist? Or was the Declaration being conflated with the Resolves?

Examine the evidence and decide for yourself by visiting the new exhibit, “Mecklenburg Declaration?” at the Presbyterian Heritage Center.

The PHC is open Tuesday-Friday (10-4) and Saturday (12-4).

title: NCMA Online Educator Course: Art and Math
description:
This self-paced, ten hour course explores points of integration between the K-8 North Carolina Essential Standards in Math and Visual Art. The course includes opportunities for educators to learn strategies for using art to identify math concepts, apply math skills to create art, and to reflect within a collaborative peer learning community. Participants will gain an understanding of best practices in arts integration and will become more familiar with the North Carolina Museum of Art’s collection.

Each course module is divided into three sections: Define, Explore, and Practice. In Define, we introduce concepts, vocabulary, and works of art to stimulate thinking and help you begin identifying points of integration between art and math. In Explore, we ask you to deeply engage in those points of integration through participating in visual thinking routines and short activities that uncover math within art. In Practice, you will engage in using math as the building blocks to create art by viewing teacher spotlight videos and exploring exemplar lesson ideas.  You will reflect on these various projects and select several that connect best with the mathematics standards that you teach, trying out those projects and planning how you would adapt them to your teaching.

The 7 Points of Integration covered in the course are:

ShapePatternSymmetryMeasurementCoordinate Points and PlanesRatio/FractionsData VisualizationThe course is aligned with the K–8 North Carolina Standard Course of Study for Visual Art and Math, which can be adapted to support foundational knowledge in secondary art and math courses. They are open to educators of all disciplines and audiences. A certificate of participation for 10 hours will be provided (1 CEU) with approval from the local school system. title: Hidden Battleship Tour
description:
Offered only four times this coming year, Hidden Battleship takes adventurous visitors beyond the traditional self-guided tour and into unrestored areas of the Battleship North Carolina Memorial that are normally closed to the public. Led by experienced guides in small groups, participants explore spaces deep below deck, throughout the third deck, in the bow, and high into the Ship's superstructure—including all the way to the top.

The 2027 Hidden Battleship tours will be offered on:

Saturday, February 27Saturday, March 20Saturday, April 24Saturday, November 20Each tour runs from 11:00 am to 5:00 pm. The cost is $75 per participant, plus tax.

Designed for adventurous history enthusiasts, the six-hour experience requires climbing ladders, crossing high hatches, and navigating tight and confined spaces. For that reason, the program is limited to participants ages 16 and older.

"Every compartment aboard the Battleship has a story," said Dr. Jay Martin, Executive Director of Battleship North Carolina Memorial. "Hidden Battleship opens doors that are normally closed, inviting visitors to step into the spaces where sailors lived, worked, and fought—and to experience the Ship in a way very few people ever will."

Because attendance is intentionally limited to provide a safe, behind-the-scenes experience, Hidden Battleship consistently sells out well in advance. The experience has become a favorite among repeat visitors, military history enthusiasts, photographers, and anyone looking to explore a side of the Ship that few ever have the opportunity to see.

Whether you're searching for a memorable gift or your next great adventure, Hidden Battleship offers an unforgettable behind-the-scenes experience unlike any other.

Visitors are encouraged to reserve their spots early. Tickets and additional information are available at https://bit.ly/hiddenbattleship

title: “To BEethoven Rather Than To Seem”: Part IV | Gut Instinct Chamber Music Project
description:
FEATURING

Nicholas DiEguenio, violin
Mimi Solomon, piano

 

PROGRAM

Featuring Beethoven’s final Violin Sonata, the elegiac and enigmatic op. 96, along with Tonia Ko’s Tribute: Axis II

This season, Gut Instinct takes on the large-scale project “To Beethoven Rather Than To Seem,” marking 200 years since Beethoven’s death and 250 since the U.S. Declaration of Independence. Over the course of five concerts, Nicholas DiEugenio and pianist Mimi Solomon will present all ten Beethoven Sonatas on period instruments along with five commissioned works written expressly for them.

This concert is presented as part of the NCHIP Festival.

 

ADMISSION

Free, no reservation required.

 

PARKING

Please plan to arrive early as parking on campus can be tricky. Learn more about parking and directions to UNC-Chapel Hill’s campus.

 

The Gut Instinct Chamber Music Project, now in its third season, is a concert series in the Triangle area which brings UNC-Chapel Hill and Duke University’s historical instrument collections together with artists committed to presenting inspired, visceral, historically informed performances of the 19th-century chamber music repertoire. The series features music of female composers and their artistic circles. The name “Gut Instinct” is a play on words. In 19th-century Europe, the violin, viola, and cello were strung with (sheep) gut.

 

All of the artists collaborating with the Pleyel and Graf pianos at UNC-Chapel Hill (built in 19th-century Paris and Vienna, respectively), as well as the Clementi piano at Duke (early 19th-century England) use these gut string materials. The turn of phrase “gut instinct” also refers to the visceral, accessible nature of the musical performances that this series presents. Our mission is to make “Historically Informed Performance” accessible, relatable, and culturally relevant! We also want to feature these special pianos that are rarely heard by the public, along with great music by female composers which has remained lesser known to the greater public for far too long, and living composers who are keeping our art form alive!

title: Gregg Museum Edition: AI Hot Topics: Does AI Have a Place in the A(a)rts?
description:
Please join the Data Science and AI Academy at the Gregg Museum of Art and Design for an exclusive AI Hot Topics event. The Gregg aims to create and hold space for the many perspectives surrounding artificial intelligence's growing presence in universities, the arts and even in our everyday lives. This hour-long conversation invites us to do more than take a side; it asks us to listen first, question and then challenge ourselves to better understand where others are coming from. 

As AI becomes increasingly present in creative spaces, questions about ethics, authorship and what may be at stake for artistic expression continue to emerge. Join us for an open conversation exploring AI's place in the arts and the possibilities and concerns that have come with it.

Artists, students, faculty and community members will unpack and share various presepctives of who gets to define art and the very real ethical concerns surrounding AI’s impact, particularly in the arts and education.
source: NC State Gregg Museum of Art & Design

title: Learning Lab: Fashion Sustainability and Makerspace
description:
Don’t throw it away, rework it.

Join the African American Cultural Center at the D.H. Hill Jr. Library Makerspace for a hands-on dive into sustainable fashion and do-it-yourself creation. Whether you want to learn the basics of how to use a sewing machine, mend your favorite damaged thrifted piece or embroider custom patches to personalize your jacket or tote, this lab is for you. We’ll cover essential mending techniques and show you how to extend the life of your wardrobe through conscious creation. Sewing experience is not necessary to participate.

We'll provide all machines and materials needed for the session. Bring a piece of clothing you’d like to mend or customize or use the practice fabric provided

If you have questions about the session, contact Andaiye Qaasim, assistant director of the African American Cultural Center, at aaqaasim@ncsu.edu.
source: NC State African American Cultural Center

title: The Surge: An Ode to Sinéad O’Connor
description:
For anyone who has ever questioned their place, pushed against expectations, or wondered what it costs to remain true to yourself, The Surge: An Ode to Sinéad O’Connor is for you.

Inspired by the music, words, and enduring spirit of Sinéad O’Connor, director and choreographer Sonya Tayeh creates a powerful dance experience performed by ten women over the age of 40. O’Connor’s music and narration, drawn from her memoir Rememberings, weave throughout the performance. 

 

The Surge is a reflection on identity, aging, freedom, and the courage required to live authentically in a world that often rewards conformity. What emerges is both deeply personal and unexpectedly communal: a celebration of women who refuse to disappear, soften themselves for others, or surrender the right to define their own lives.

 

Student tickets always $11. Eligible for CLE. Find out more and buy tickets at: https://carolinaperformingarts.org/events/the-surge/

title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians
description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority,  and is published that it may go down to posterity.”  

The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.

But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting. No extant copies could be found.

The debate over the authenticity of the Mecklenburg Declaration began. And, when a copy of a document called the Mecklenburg Resolves written on May 30, 1775, was discovered in a 1775 newspaper, the debate intensified. The Resolves were revolutionary, but stopped short of declaring independence. Did both documents exist? Or was the Declaration being conflated with the Resolves?

Examine the evidence and decide for yourself by visiting the new exhibit, “Mecklenburg Declaration?” at the Presbyterian Heritage Center.

The PHC is open Tuesday-Friday (10-4) and Saturday (12-4).

title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians
description:

But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting. No extant copies could be found.

title: Foundations of Applied Mixed Methods Research Design
description:

title: The Vijay Iyer Quartet
description:
Some performances—especially jazz—invite you to surrender the need to know what’s coming next. You stop trying to predict the next note and simply hold your breath, waiting to discover where the music will lead. That uncertainty is the thrill: performers and audience alike following the sound somewhere unexpected, until you find yourself wondering, How did they do that?

 

The Vijay Iyer Quartet lives in that space of possibility. Performing compositions by composer-pianist Vijay Iyer, the ensemble reveals new possibilities in the music each time it takes the stage.

 

Voted DownBeat‘s Jazz Artist of the Year four times and a MacArthur Fellow, Iyer has spent decades expanding the possibilities of the jazz quartet. His celebrated trio with bassist Linda May Han Oh and drummer Tyshawn Sorey was praised by The New York Times as “one of the best bands in jazz.”

 

Building on three decades of musical collaboration and experimentation, Iyer expanded the ensemble in 2025 with the addition of trumpeter Adam O’Farrill, a longtime collaborator and member of one of Afro-Latin music’s most revered musical families.

 

Together, the quartet combines acoustic instruments with Fender Rhodes and electronics, creating music that is fearless, unpredictable, and constantly unfolding.

 

Student tickets always $11. Eligible for CLE. Find out more and buy tickets at: https://carolinaperformingarts.org/events/thevijayiyerquartet/

title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians
description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority,  and is published that it may go down to posterity.”  

The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.

But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting. No extant copies could be found.

The debate over the authenticity of the Mecklenburg Declaration began. And, when a copy of a document called the Mecklenburg Resolves written on May 30, 1775, was discovered in a 1775 newspaper, the debate intensified. The Resolves were revolutionary, but stopped short of declaring independence. Did both documents exist? Or was the Declaration being conflated with the Resolves?

Examine the evidence and decide for yourself by visiting the new exhibit, “Mecklenburg Declaration?” at the Presbyterian Heritage Center.

The PHC is open Tuesday-Friday (10-4) and Saturday (12-4).

title: NCMA Online Educator Course: Art and Math
description:
This self-paced, ten hour course explores points of integration between the K-8 North Carolina Essential Standards in Math and Visual Art. The course includes opportunities for educators to learn strategies for using art to identify math concepts, apply math skills to create art, and to reflect within a collaborative peer learning community. Participants will gain an understanding of best practices in arts integration and will become more familiar with the North Carolina Museum of Art’s collection.

Each course module is divided into three sections: Define, Explore, and Practice. In Define, we introduce concepts, vocabulary, and works of art to stimulate thinking and help you begin identifying points of integration between art and math. In Explore, we ask you to deeply engage in those points of integration through participating in visual thinking routines and short activities that uncover math within art. In Practice, you will engage in using math as the building blocks to create art by viewing teacher spotlight videos and exploring exemplar lesson ideas.  You will reflect on these various projects and select several that connect best with the mathematics standards that you teach, trying out those projects and planning how you would adapt them to your teaching.

The 7 Points of Integration covered in the course are:

ShapePatternSymmetryMeasurementCoordinate Points and PlanesRatio/FractionsData VisualizationThe course is aligned with the K–8 North Carolina Standard Course of Study for Visual Art and Math, which can be adapted to support foundational knowledge in secondary art and math courses. They are open to educators of all disciplines and audiences. A certificate of participation for 10 hours will be provided (1 CEU) with approval from the local school system. The course runs from January 27th - April 6th and educators can join at any point. Registration is now open. $18 Members, $20 Nonmembers.

title: Hidden Battleship Tour
description:
Offered only four times this coming year, Hidden Battleship takes adventurous visitors beyond the traditional self-guided tour and into unrestored areas of the Battleship North Carolina Memorial that are normally closed to the public. Led by experienced guides in small groups, participants explore spaces deep below deck, throughout the third deck, in the bow, and high into the Ship's superstructure—including all the way to the top.

The 2027 Hidden Battleship tours will be offered on:

Saturday, March 20Saturday, April 24Saturday, November 20Each tour runs from 11:00 am to 5:00 pm. The cost is $75 per participant, plus tax.

Designed for adventurous history enthusiasts, the six-hour experience requires climbing ladders, crossing high hatches, and navigating tight and confined spaces. For that reason, the program is limited to participants ages 16 and older.

Because attendance is intentionally limited to provide a safe, behind-the-scenes experience, Hidden Battleship consistently sells out well in advance. The experience has become a favorite among repeat visitors, military history enthusiasts, photographers, and anyone looking to explore a side of the Ship that few ever have the opportunity to see.

Whether you're searching for a memorable gift or your next great adventure, Hidden Battleship offers an unforgettable behind-the-scenes experience unlike any other.

Visitors are encouraged to reserve their spots early. Tickets and additional information are available at https://bit.ly/hiddenbattleship

This self-paced, ten hour course explores points of integration between the K-8 North Carolina Essential Standards in Math and Visual Art. The course includes opportunities for educators to learn strategies for using art to identify math concepts, apply math skills to create art, and to reflect within a collaborative peer learning community. Participants will gain an understanding of best practices in arts integration and will become more familiar with the North Carolina Museum of Art’s collection.

Each course module is divided into three sections: Define, Explore, and Practice. In Define, we introduce concepts, vocabulary, and works of art to stimulate thinking and help you begin identifying points of integration between art and math. In Explore, we ask you to deeply engage in those points of integration through participating in visual thinking routines and short activities that uncover math within art. In Practice, you will engage in using math as the building blocks to create art by viewing teacher spotlight videos and exploring exemplar lesson ideas.  You will reflect on these various projects and select several that connect best with the mathematics standards that you teach, trying out those projects and planning how you would adapt them to your teaching.

The 7 Points of Integration covered in the course are:

ShapePatternSymmetryMeasurementCoordinate Points and PlanesRatio/FractionsData VisualizationThe course is aligned with the K–8 North Carolina Standard Course of Study for Visual Art and Math, which can be adapted to support foundational knowledge in secondary art and math courses. They are open to educators of all disciplines and audiences. A certificate of participation for 10 hours will be provided (1 CEU) with approval from the local school system. The course runs from January 27th - April 6th and educators can join at any point. Registration is now open. $18 Members, $20 Nonmembers.

title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians
description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority,  and is published that it may go down to posterity.”  

The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.

But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting. No extant copies could be found.

The debate over the authenticity of the Mecklenburg Declaration began. And, when a copy of a document called the Mecklenburg Resolves written on May 30, 1775, was discovered in a 1775 newspaper, the debate intensified. The Resolves were revolutionary, but stopped short of declaring independence. Did both documents exist? Or was the Declaration being conflated with the Resolves?

Examine the evidence and decide for yourself by visiting the new exhibit, “Mecklenburg Declaration?” at the Presbyterian Heritage Center.

The PHC is open Tuesday-Friday (10-4) and Saturday (12-4).

title: Introduction to Stata
description:
This course introduces students to Stata and data management. It is tailored for non-users who want to learn how to manage data more effectively. Each day, the class will demonstrate how to use the commands, followed by hands-on exercises using sample datasets. By the end of the course, participants will be able to perform the following:

 

• Use Stata’s Graphical User Interference (GUI) with dialog boxes
• Run Stata commands from the command window and from scripts (“do” files)
• Enter, transfer, and save data in different formats, e.g., Excel, SAS, SPSS, text files
• Inspect the contents of a Stata dataset
• Append, merge, and sort datasets
• Identify and clean duplicate records
• Calculate new variables
• Create and manage labels for variables and values
• Recode variables
• Work with blocks of observations (“by” processing)
• Perform row-wise calculations (groups of columns)
• Collapse data into summary tables
• Reshape between long and wide formats
• Save and reproduce your work with “do” files
• Obtain descriptive statistics
• Create graphs and tables
• Run basic statistical analyses, e.g., Ordinary Least Squares regression, correlation matrices, Chi-square tests, t-tests

 

Registration and fee (refundable for UNC-Chapel Hill students upon attendance) are required for Zoom link access.

Hand Away Your Resume: Print multiple copies of your resume so employers/schools can quite literally have it on file.

title: Che Apalache
description:
What do you get when you blend Appalachian bluegrass and old-time music with Latin American folk traditions including flamenco, murga, and candombe? You get Che Apalache’s acclaimed Latingrass! 

 

Founder Joe Troop grew up in North Carolina and taught music in Buenos Aires after graduating from UNC. His students became his bandmates: Pau Barjau on banjo, Franco Martino on guitar, and Omar Ruiz-Lopez on mandolin.

 

Rooted in traditions that span continents, the band grew out of a willingness to follow interests across languages, cultures, and traditions. What emerged is a sound shaped by relationships, shared experiences, and a genuine openness to learning from one another.

 

Student tickets always $11. Eligible for CLE. Find out more and buy tickets at: https://carolinaperformingarts.org/events/cheapalache/

title: Introduction to Stata
description:
This course introduces students to Stata and data management. It is tailored for non-users who want to learn how to manage data more effectively. Each day, the class will demonstrate how to use the commands, followed by hands-on exercises using sample datasets. By the end of the course, participants will be able to perform the following:

 

• Use Stata’s Graphical User Interference (GUI) with dialog boxes
• Run Stata commands from the command window and from scripts (“do” files)
• Enter, transfer, and save data in different formats, e.g., Excel, SAS, SPSS, text files
• Inspect the contents of a Stata dataset
• Append, merge, and sort datasets
• Identify and clean duplicate records
• Calculate new variables
• Create and manage labels for variables and values
• Recode variables
• Work with blocks of observations (“by” processing)
• Perform row-wise calculations (groups of columns)
• Collapse data into summary tables
• Reshape between long and wide formats
• Save and reproduce your work with “do” files
• Obtain descriptive statistics
• Create graphs and tables
• Run basic statistical analyses, e.g., Ordinary Least Squares regression, correlation matrices, Chi-square tests, t-tests

 

Registration and fee (refundable for UNC-Chapel Hill students upon attendance) are required for Zoom link access.

title: Sold Out: Educator Trek: Secrets of the Swamp
location: North Carolina Museum of Natural Sciences
description:
Explore North Carolina’s bottomland hardwood forest and experience a night in a remote swamp. We will camp on the Roanoke River Partner’s platforms in the homes of beaver, barred owls, and migratory songbirds. Go to sleep to the hootin’ and hollerin’ of barred owls and wake to the sweet call of prothonotary warblers. Become familiar with one of North Carolina’s true wild areas and bring new ideas and activities back to your students. The Museum has tents, sleeping pads, ground chairs, and a few sleeping bags to loan if you don’t have your own camping gear!

Credit: 16 contact hours toward CEUs or Criteria II/III for North Carolina’s Environmental Education Certification Program

Lodging: The workshop fee covers one night of platform camping in tents on the Roanoke River near Jamesville, NC

Transportation: Participants will ride with the group from Raleigh departing at 8am. Transportation will be in Museum vans or bus.

Registration: This workshop is FULL, please join our waiting list!

The full workshop fee is due when you register and payment is via credit card. Registration for most Educator Treks is on a first-come, first-served basis. Treks fill quickly, so register early! If when you attempt to register it is full, please join our waiting list and we will notify you as soon as possible if a space opens for you!

Note: We do not want cost to be a barrier for any educator. If the cost of this workshop would prevent your participation, please reach out to Megan Davis.

Details:

Fee: $115 (includes canoe rental, camping platform fee, most meals, most camping gear)Requirements: For educators (includes teachers, administrators, pre-service or substitute teachers; non-formal educators; any adult working on their EE certification)Program Instructor(s): Megan Davis, Rory McCollumActivity Level: Moderate

You will reflect on these various projects and select several that connect best with the mathematics standards that you teach, trying out those projects and planning how you would adapt them to your teaching.

The 7 Points of Integration covered in the course are:

ShapePatternSymmetryMeasurementCoordinate Points and PlanesRatio/FractionsData VisualizationThe course is aligned with the K–8 North Carolina Standard Course of Study for Visual Art and Math, which can be adapted to support foundational knowledge in secondary art and math courses. They are open to educators of all disciplines and audiences. A certificate of participation for 10 hours will be provided (1 CEU) with approval from the local school system. The course runs from January 27th - April 6th and educators can join at any point. Registration is now open. $18 Members, $20 Nonmembers.

title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians
description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority,  and is published that it may go down to posterity.”  

The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.

But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting. No extant copies could be found.

The debate over the authenticity of the Mecklenburg Declaration began. And, when a copy of a document called the Mecklenburg Resolves written on May 30, 1775, was discovered in a 1775 newspaper, the debate intensified. The Resolves were revolutionary, but stopped short of declaring independence. Did both documents exist? Or was the Declaration being conflated with the Resolves?

Examine the evidence and decide for yourself by visiting the new exhibit, “Mecklenburg Declaration?” at the Presbyterian Heritage Center.

The PHC is open Tuesday-Friday (10-4) and Saturday (12-4).

title: NC Public Librarian Certification Commission
description:
The NC Public Librarian Certification Commission was formed in 1936 to set minimum standards for public librarians to protect and maintain public library resources, to assure professional management and administration of library services, to meet the personnel requirements for State Aid administered by the Library of NC, and to guarantee the best possible public library service to all North Carolinians.

The North Carolina General Statute 143B-68 states that the commission must be comprised of: the Chairman of the public libraries section of NCLA, two individuals named by the Governor upon nomination of the NCLA, the dean of a State or regionally accredited graduate school of librarianship in North Carolina appointed by the Governor, and one member at large appointed by the Governor. Commission members appointed by the Governor serve 4-year terms, all others serve 2-year terms.

Commission meetings are held quarterly to review applications and discuss Certification policies and procedures.

The commission's meeting dates for the 2025-2026 year are October 27, 2025, January 9, 2026, April 10, 2026, and July 10, 2026. All meetings are held at the Library of NC beginning at 1:00 pm unless otherwise posted. Information about meetings can be found on the North Carolina Secretary of State's meeting calendar.

Have questions about certification? Contact us at NC.Certification.Commission@dncr.nc.gov.

title: NC State LIVE Well-Being Concerts With Nnenna and Pierce Freelon
location: Gregg Museum of Art & Design, Galleries and Main Lobby
description:
NC State LIVE and the Gregg Museum of Art & Design have partnered to present Well-Being Concerts, featuring a family with rich connections to the university and the museum. The late architect Phil Freelon, an NC State College of Design alumnus, led the team that designed the Gregg’s new home, which opened in 2017. Phil Freelon's widow and son, Nnenna and Pierce Freelon, are a Grammy-nominated mother-son musical duo known for their collaborative children’s album, AnceStars. Nnenna Freelon is an acclaimed composer, podcaster, author and advocate for arts education. In addition to his music career, Pierce Freelon is a picture book author, podcaster and ice cream maker. The duo will perform at the Gregg inside the gallery featuring the exhibition Grounded by artist-in-residence Maya Freelon, Phil and Nnenna Freelon’s daughter. Shaped by Maya Freelon’s personal and collective memory, ancestry and humanity, Grounded transforms the Gregg into a retrospective on well-being, connection and discovery. 

This concert was created in partnership with Carnegie Hall’s Weill Music Institute. Carnegie Hall’s Well-Being Concerts combine world-class musical performances with elements of self-care and mindfulness, animated by evidence that music helps people heal and thrive.
source: NC State Gregg Museum of Art & Design

description: This exhibit explores how North Carolina helped forge a new nation during one of the most transformative periods in history. Through maps, historical documents, and everyday objects, this exhibit reveals the state’s role in the struggle for independence, from early protests against British rule and the battles fought on Carolina soil to the drafting of the Constitution. Forging a Nation invites visitors to witness how ordinary people, conflict, and conviction shaped North Carolina's history during the American Revolution.

title: Introduction to Focus Groups
description:
Focus groups are commonly used to capture rich information about attitudes and beliefs. This class will prepare prospective students to organize and moderate focus groups. Students will learn the most appropriate uses of focus groups, how to segment and recruit audiences, how to develop a moderator’s guide, and how to moderate focus groups. The class will be supplemented with real-life examples and hands-on exercises.

Registration and fee (refundable for UNCCH students upon attendance of course) are required for Zoom link access.
